Two men were arrested following a nearly monthlong investigation into a string of car burglaries across neighborhoods in Martin County. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office announced the arrests of Stephen Ivan Morris and Shaun Alexander Bilbrey. Both face 36 charges of grand theft, armed burglary, larceny and traveling to commit a burglary. Both were booked into the Martin County Jail on Tuesday. "This probably started with a handful of a few mistakes, and then it escalated rapidly. These kids are in real trouble. They've done a lot of damage in a short period of time, in a one month period of time. For here and now, they've ruined their current life, and they've ruined it for the next couple years as they go through the court system and the prison system, probably," said John Budensiek, Martin Co. See also: Dolly Parton's legacy lives on in Palm Beach County through Imagination Library The investigation into burglaries affecting multiple neighborhoods, including gated communities, began in early August. With assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office SWAT team and Criminal Investigations Division, Martin County detectives served warrants at the St. Lucie County homes of Morris, 19, and Bilbrey, 19. "None of these were scenarios where they forced their way into the cars. They were simply pulling on door handles and grabbing what was easy to get," Budensiek said. The two men allegedly committed 15 burglaries and stole at least 7 firearms. They also allegedly committed a burglary when they went into an open garage and stole a golf cart and drove it around the neighborhood to commit car burglaries. The car burglaries happened in Hobe Sound, Palm City and two areas in Stuart, including the Stuart Yacht and Country Club. Sheriff Budensiek says the two men may have committed other car burglaries too, that have not been reported yet because the victims are unaware their cars were burglarized. "We have one firearm that was stolen in Hobe Sound, and then traded, according to these young men at a gas station for some cash or some kind of a transaction, and we don't know where that is. If you're the one that has that firearm, we want you to know that it's stolen. You won't be in trouble if you bring it back to us. But if we catch you with it, that'll be a whole different ball game," Budensiek explained. The Sheriff says he has a message for firearm owners. "If you're going to keep a firearm in a car, which is not a good idea to start with, lock your car," he said.

Vero Beach utility customers will face significant bill increases over the next four years after both the city’s Utility Commission and City Council unanimously approved a comprehensive rate increase plan to fund major infrastructure improvements. The Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to increase water and sewer rates beginning on Oct. A typical residential customer using 4,000 gallons per month currently pays $83.54 for combined water and sewer service. By 2029, that same bill will reach $122.45 monthly — an increase of nearly $39 per month, or 46.7% over current rates. The rate increases stem from a $217 million capital improvement program planned through 2030, according to city documents. The centerpiece is a new Water Reclamation Facility currently under construction in Vero Beach. To finance the project, the city plans to issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027. The bonds are structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate, creating average annual debt service of approximately $8.66 million. An additional $42.3 million in grants will also support the project. The bond amount represents a significant jump from earlier projections. A 2022 rate study anticipated an $80 million bond issuance, but that figure has grown by $45 million due to cost escalation. Water rates will increase 10% in fiscal year 2027, 7.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 5% in each of the following two years, according to the approved schedule. Wastewater rates face steeper increases: 15% in both fiscal years 2027 and 2028, 10% in 2029, and 5% in 2030. Reclaimed water customers will see the largest percentage increases at 25% in both 2027 and 2028, followed by 5% annual increases. Beyond capital construction, the utility’s operating expenses continue climbing at an average annual rate of 4.1%. Operating costs will grow from approximately $25.6 million in fiscal year 2026 to more than $32 million by 2030. Rate consultants at Raftelis identified additional operating costs of $3.07 million in fiscal year 2026 and $4.9 million in fiscal year 2029 compared to the prior 2022 rate study. Currently, Vero Beach’s combined bill of $83.54 falls below the regional average of $89.47 for similar usage, according to the Raftelis study. However, once the 2027 increases take effect, Vero Beach’s $107.30 bill will exceed several neighboring utilities. Fort Pierce Utilities Authority currently charges $95.76 for the same 4,000-gallon usage level. Indian River County Sewer bills $67.70 for comparable service. The ordinance creates a new Wastewater Readiness-to-Serve Charge affecting property owners who receive city water service but use septic tanks while having public wastewater service available nearby. The charge starts at $40.85 monthly for typical residential customers as of Oct. 1, rising to $54.24 monthly by Oct. Property owners receive 75 days notice before the charge takes effect. According to city documents, the charge applies in lieu of standard wastewater user charges for properties not yet connected to the public system. New rates take effect Oct. 1, with subsequent annual adjustments each Oct. The final public hearing for ordinance adoption was held on Tuesday. The rate increases reflect Vero Beach’s commitment to upgrading aging infrastructure while maintaining compliance with environmental regulations governing water treatment and distribution systems. A Colorado doctor accused of opening fire on federal agents during an attempted arrest in Vero Beach has been indicted on multiple federal charges, according to the U.S. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 A federal grand jury on Thursday indicted 72-year-old Thomas Steffans in connection with a March shooting involving deputy U.S. marshals on the Treasure Coast. Investigators said Steffans was wanted in Grand Junction, Colorado, and traveled by bus to Vero Beach in early March. Students at Central Elementary School in Okeechobee are participating in the revived Presidential Physical Fitness Test after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to reestablish it in schools.The origins of the Presidential Physical Fitness Test date back to 1958. That's when the American Alliance for Health, Physical Education and Recreation (AAHPER) created the Youth Fitness Project, which introduced the first standardized national fitness test in the U.S.WATCH BELOW: Trump's executive order brings presidential fitness test back to local schoolsThe original test consisted of pull-ups for boys and modified pull-ups for girls, sit-ups, a shuttle run, standing long jump, 50-yard dash and softball throw for distance. In 1966, President Lyndon B. Johnson established the Presidential Physical Fitness Award Program. Over the years, the test went through changes before it was essentially retired in 2012 under the administration of President Barack Obama. Now, a whole new generation is experiencing the revived test for the first time.According to the White House website, the Presidential Fitness Test provides students with clear, age-appropriate benchmarks that encourage them to build strength, endurance and healthy habits while striving for personal improvement. The standards are based on a combination of historical fitness benchmarks and additional fitness data, creating meaningful goals that are both challenging and achievable.The White House says two levels of achievement — Presidential and National — recognize students who meet established fitness benchmarks, while all students who complete the test may receive a Certificate of Participation. Together, these recognition levels encourage students to set goals, track progress, and celebrate their accomplishments.Coach Spearow, a physical education coach at Central Elementary, said the test's return is significant regardless of how people feel about the president who brought it back."It is something President Trump, whether you love him or hate him, has brought back," Spearow said.Spearow also reflected on what the test was like for those who took it in previous generations."It was brutal," Spearow said.He also pointed to a shift in how kids spend their time today compared to previous generations."These kids go home and get on their phones, computers, and play video games. They don't get outside and play like our generation did," Spearow said.The new test format pushes students to develop strength and endurance based on age and gender."We can either do pushups or pullups, we can do planks or situps; then the pacer test or the mile run," Spearow said.Before the test began, students warmed up with stretching, squats, and mountain climbers. Then came push-ups, planks and running — giving mixed reactions from fourth graders."It was hard," one student said.Another fourth-grade student had a different take, flexing his muscles and saying he enjoys the test because he likes to workout, which made the test easy.Students will test again as the school year continues.Not every school district in the area is following suit. Lucie County Schools said it is not aware of any schools in the district conducting the test. Indian River County Schools had not responded yet.Palm Beach County Schools provided the statement below on its approach to physical education."District-operated schools follow the physical educational standards and benchmarks set forth by the Florida Department of Education. Florida statutes establish physical education time requirements rather than a statewide mandated fitness assessment, leaving specific testing guidelines up to individual school discretion"This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A major transition inside Fort Pierce's legal department is raising questions about who will help guide the city through several high-profile development issues expected to come before the City Commission. The uncertainty follows the City Commission's decision not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract. At the same time, Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman has resigned, and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month, leaving the city searching for new legal leadership. This week, commissioners voted 3-2 to move forward with appointing Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while a search is conducted for a permanent replacement. For Commissioner Michael Broderick, the concern isn't just staffing. He argues the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions. "There are several very volatile projects that are slated to come in front of the city commission in short order, and we really have no independent legal representation to be able to deal with that on behalf of the city commission, in my opinion," Broderick told CBS12 News. Broderick pointed specifically to future development proposals on South Hutchinson Island. Among the issues he expects to surface are potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. Broderick said removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island. The debate over development was one of several issues discussed as commissioners considered Wallace's appointment. See also: 2 arrested in string of car burglaries in Martin County Wallace previously worked in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager. Supporters said that experience makes her well-positioned to step into the role and help keep city business moving while a nationwide search for a permanent city attorney gets underway. Broderick voted against the appointment. "So what the city commission did against my protests is they appointed the assistant city manager to now be a charter officer in the city of Fort Pierce," Broderick said. "In my opinion, that reeks of duplicity and multiple bosses you need to report to. I'm not sure how that is even possible to do." Supporters of the move countered that Wallace's legal background and familiarity with city operations provide continuity at a time when the city is losing much of its legal staff. Meanwhile, the commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Renée Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney. The agreement authorizes up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process. City officials expect the interim appointment to return to the commission in the form of a formal contract and resolution. The search for a permanent city attorney is expected to continue over the coming months.

Repeated flooding on Ocean Drive in Vero Beach is raising concerns among business owners, and the city says a permanent fix could cost millions of dollars and take years to complete.Lee Olsen, general manager at Waldo's Restaurant and Bar, sent WPTV a video of the flooding on Ocean Drive after Wednesday's storm. He said it was among the worst he has seen.WATCH BELOW: Flooding on Ocean Drive leaves businesses struggling "I've been here 20 years," Olsen said. "Probably one of the worst floodings I've seen."Olsen said the water level was high."When I walked out into the middle of the street, the water was up to my knees," he said.Wednesday was not the first time this week the road flooded."We had the same thing happen on Monday," Olsen said.Olsen said the flooding has become a recurring problem tied to the area's daily weather pattern."Every afternoon we get a thunderstorm. Every afternoon we possibly will end up dealing with flooding," Olsen said.The flooding has also created dangerous conditions for Olsen and his staff after their shifts."I drove down Ocean Drive yesterday to get my employee to their car because the water was so deep; I almost lost my car," Olsen said.Across the street, Aubrey Moxley and Leah Trodglen work at Allure Gallery. Moxley said the flooding builds quickly."It doesn't matter how long it rains for; that water is collecting," Moxley said. "This entire street flooded in less than 30 minutes of rain."Moxley said the flooding is a threat to businesses along the strip."They can't go to the beach, they can't come and shop," Moxley said. "It definitely can be crippling for businesses on Ocean Drive."Moxley said the severity is new."I have never seen the street flood the way that it has been this past week," she said.Olsen said he is worried about what a major storm could bring."These ground-level businesses would end up being flooded, and that's unacceptable," Olsen said. "It needs to be addressed by the city."WPTV reached out to the City of Vero Beach Public Works Department for answers. Staff said the pump stations and other drainage infrastructure were working but are only designed to handle 1 inch of rainfall per hour. The most recent storms exceeded that, delivering 2 or more inches of rainfall in an hour.To fix the flooding, staff said it would require rebuilding the road and making drainage improvements — a project that could cost millions of dollars and take years to complete.Olsen acknowledged the scale of the challenge."It's a big financial endeavor," Olsen said. "Where do you say too much money versus damage to local businesses?"Public works staff said there is no improvement project planned for Ocean Drive at this time.

More than a month after fire ripped through her Vero Beach home, Debbie Drennan said she received a bill from Florida Power Light charging her for electricity for weeks after her power had been cut off. The fire started in the early morning hours of July 5, destroying the home's carport and kitchen. “I’ve never been through anything like this. I mean, it was traumatic,” Drennan said. Drennan said the situation worsened a month later when she received a bill for power, including for the time after they had no service. And I’m like, 'What?' So, I looked at the dates, and it was after the fire. There was no electricity whatsoever,” she said. Drennan said she called FPL multiple times but could not get answers. She added that the company even contacted her to say they were coming to disconnect her service for nonpayment. Well, you just come on.' So, when he got here, I’m like, 'Sir, what are you disconnecting? Because there’s nothing to disconnect,'” Drennan said. After WPBF 25 News contacted FPL on Wednesday, the company said it could not discuss a customer’s account but later reached out to Drennan. In an email, FPL apologized for the frustration and explained that the charge was due to an "estimated bill" because their "system could not communicate" with her meter. That meter was melted during the fire. The company agreed to remove the charge. "At least the $922 is gone. Thanks to you guys.” Drennan said now that the issue with FPL has been resolved, she and her family can focus on repairing their home. Martin County commissioners are moving toward a potential pause on data center development after several residents showed up at a commission meeting Tuesday to voice concerns about hyperscale facilities and their impact on the community. Commissioners voted 4-1 to place a discussion of a possible moratorium on data center development considerations on the agenda for their next meeting. If approved, the pause would give commissioners time to determine what rules and regulations they want to impose on data center projects. WATCH: Martin County eyes pause on data center development Martin County resident Ann Vandersteel said she worries the nationwide surge in hyperscale data center development threatens the character of her community. "My biggest fear is that they're going to disrupt that — they're going to turn my beautiful rural Martin County into a hyperscale data center campus," Vandersteel said. She and other residents urged commissioners to act before projects move forward. "What are we willing to sacrifice to power this AI intelligence economy?" Vandersteel said. Other residents echoed those concerns during public comment. "Martin County is not an industrial sacrifice zone," one resident said. "Residents should not have to discover the consequences after the project has been approved and built," another resident said. "A lot of people are worried and concerned and rightfully so. So I think as commissioners it's imperative that you do your homework," a third resident said. Residents raised concerns about the impact data centers could have on air quality, noise pollution, water usage and electrical infrastructure. "Those are the key, key issues from where I'm sitting, environmental, property values, who pays for it because those all have impacts nobody wants some industrial sized park right across from their home," Vandersteel said. "Get ahead of it now, don't wait." Commissioner Edward Ciampi called for a moratorium during the meeting. "I want staff to bring forward an agenda item for a moratorium giving us the opportunity to have that year to then bring forward the experts and opinions to have it, but we have to push the pause button first," Ciampi said. Commissioner Eileen Vargas noted the timeline could be flexible depending on how the review unfolds. "It's not hard and fast one year if we have to continue looking at more information because this is an evolving subject," Vargas said. Vandersteel said she left the meeting feeling cautiously optimistic. "That to me was very encouraging. They were asking the right questions," Vandersteel said. A federal judge on Thursday halted — at least for now — attempts to implement President Donald Trump’s executive order limiting mail voting.The move stalled the directive for a second time only about a week before the first mail ballots are due to be sent out for the rapidly approaching midterm elections. District Court Judge Indira Talwani blocked the government from implementing the order for two weeks.The case could soon be appealed back to the Supreme Court, days after the justices handed down a procedural decision that allowed the the administration to move ahead.RELATED STORY | Supreme Court clears the way for Trump mail voting order in advance of midtermsThe ruling Thursday came after Democrats and voting rights groups refiled their lawsuits to comply with the recent Supreme Court decision. The high court's conservative majority did not rule on the legality of Trump’s executive order, instead saying Talwani had acted too soon.Now the administration has issued a formal rule governing whether the U.S. Postal Service will deliver states’ mail ballots, effectively restarting the legal fight.The whipsawing legal battle has major ramifications for the midterms. Nearly one-third of Americans vote by mail and election officials contend there isn’t enough time to revise their systems to comply with the new Postal Service directives.The Postal Service says it won’t deliver mail ballots unless states provide a list of voters who should receive them and format the envelopes in a certain way.“Plaintiff states have neither time nor funds to design new mail ballots, seek approval of the new designs, order production of mail ballots, update their own election management systems, train election officials to use the USPS portal and upload citizen data to the portal, all before the midterms," Talwani wrote Thursday.RELATED STORY | Trump casts Florida ballot by mail after calling for limits on mail votingThe White House did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment. A hearing in the case is set for Sept. 3.“This rule is a clear attempt by the federal government to interfere in elections it has no power to control. Today, a federal court halted it before this administration could wreak havoc on our elections,” New York Attorney General Letitia James, one of two dozen Democratic attorneys general who filed one of the suits, said in a statement after the order.Democrats and voting rights groups contend the Postal Services' demand is unconstitutional. The Constitution, they note, grants states and, in some cases, Congress the power to make election rules — not the president or Postal Service.That reasoning led courts to block Trump’s first executive order, issued last year, that sought to change election procedures, such as requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register.The president has long targeted mail voting, which he falsely blames for his 2020 election loss even though he himself uses it to cast his ballot.A report by the Brookings Institution published in 2025 found that mail voting fraud occurred in only about four cases out of every 10 million mail ballots cast.Trump issued the executive order targeting mail voting, his second one related to elections since he returned to office, in March.Opponents quickly sued, but the administration argued the claims were premature because it hadn’t issued rules outlining how it would implement the order. The administration won an initial case in Washington, D.C., with that reasoning, but Talwani placed injunctions against implementing the order for the November midterms in two separate cases she heard in Boston.The Supreme Court’s conservative majority on Monday struck down one of those holds.Talwani, nominated to the bench by President Barack Obama, reluctantly removed the second injunction shortly after. The plaintiffs then moved to refile their cases, citing the Postal Service’s publishing of its final rule, in hopes of winning a more durable victory.

Lucie neighborhood are cleaning up after an EF-0 tornado touched down Sunday, and some say the weather alerts meant to warn them either arrived too late — or never came at all.The National Weather Service issued a Tornado Warning for portions of St. after the initial tornado reports in Port St. Lucie.Watch report from Zitali SolacheAron Christiansen said his alert came in at 6:28 p.m., 6 minutes after the tornado had already passed his home."It's crazy like, I got the tornado alert after it hit my house. Was outside looking around and got the alert its like tornado warning, yeah, no kidding," Christiansen said.One day after the storm, Christiansen was already working to clear the damage."Made progress getting some of the lanai down," Christiansen said.He described the difference between preparing for a hurricane versus a tornado."Hurricanes — we get days to prepare, and tornado we had all of 10 seconds," Christiansen said.Neighbor Theresa Garone said she never received an alert."It's scary, it is, cause we don't get any warning for that," Garone said."My nephews phone went off for a tornado, but my phone never went off. so I don't know if it was like — I don't know what happened," Garone said.The NWS said about 145,000 people were in the Tornado Warning area, though the agency does not track how many individuals ultimately received alerts through the various dissemination systems.Once issued, the warning was distributed through multiple channels, including NOAA Weather Radio, the Emergency Alert System on television and radio, Wireless Emergency Alerts on compatible mobile devices, and local notification services such as ALERT St. The NWS said the exact time an individual receives an alert can vary depending on the dissemination system, cellular provider, device settings, and local notification service.The NWS said it had no known technical or dissemination issues with its systems related to this warning. Officials said the tornado was a small, shallow circulation that was not well-sampled by radar. Unlike stronger tornadoes associated with rotating thunderstorms, landspouts typically develop from rotation near the ground that stretches upward beneath a developing thunderstorm. Because these circulations can be very small and short-lived, they can be difficult for radar to detect — particularly at greater distances from the radar site.In comparison, the NWS said radar can often detect tornadoes associated with stronger, deeper rotation within a thunderstorm higher in the atmosphere before a tornado develops at the ground, sometimes providing more advance warning. Atmospheric conditions at the time remained favorable for the development of additional landspouts or waterspouts in the area.Last year, investigative reporter Kate Hussey uncovered flaws in Florida's tornado alert system, where thousands of people received alerts too late as a tornado struck Martin County in October 2024.Resident Scott Appell said timely alerts matter."From what I saw, that is important," Appell said.Appell acknowledged that while improvements could be made, the unpredictable nature of weather presents its own challenges."Technology can always be improved," Appell said. "I just don't know how it's going to be fast enough to relay to people."

A drinking water warning is in place in Okeechobee after the Okeechobee Utility Authority found high levels of lead in water samples taken from nine homes. Officials say the lead sampling was part of routine monitoring — and that it remains unknown whether more homes are impacted. The utility will continue sampling to determine the source, officials said.WATCH: Okeechobee families demand answers as lead is found in drinking water at 9 homesFor resident Sierra Casian, a mother of five boys, the warning hit close to home."Kind of nerve-wracking that our water isn't even safe," Casian said.Her family relies on water constantly — at home, at school and everywhere in between."They're always drinking water from somewhere — whether it's the hose or I mean they go through school. I send them with water and they come back they gotta constantly get water," Casian said.The Okeechobee Utility Authority tested 70 water samples between June and July as part of the routine monitoring, finding high lead levels at the nine homes. Officials say the source of the lead is likely plumbing, pipes or fixtures at individual properties — not the broader water supply. Pediatrician flagged concerns months agoCasian said her pediatrician first raised concerns in May, warning that children in her baby's age group had shown elevated lead levels and recommending bloodwork."They said that he needed to get the bloodwork to be tested for lead because a bunch of kids in his age group had elevated lead levels. And that was shocking," Casian said.Her baby was fortunately not exposed.A follow-up exam was requested for the beginning of August. Casian said no testing was ever requested for her four other children.What lead exposure can do to the bodyDr. Celina Moore of Moore Healthy Kids and Palm Beach Health Network said families should take two immediate steps."I ask them to do two things, test the water and test the child," Moore said.Moore explained that lead exposure can cause serious harm. Acute intoxication — where a large amount of lead enters the body in a short period — can affect both adults and children, leading to cardiac abnormalities, brain issues and damage to other organs. Chronic low-level exposure can be harder to detect but may cause decreased IQ, behavioral problems and loss of attention.Ingestion is the most common cause of exposure, whether through drinking water or contact with toys containing lead."For most cases of low lead exposure — just removal of the source of lead from consumption is enough for the body to clear the lead on its own. For higher levels, there are therapies. It's called chelation — those are done by doctors in order to bind the lead in the system and have the body excrete it," Moore said.Moore also noted that lead cannot be detected without testing. "Lead in water is tasteless, odorless, has no color to it so you don't know if your water has lead unless you test it," Moore said.What families can do nowThe Okeechobee Utility Authority says water testing is available through the agency and that proper water filters can help reduce lead exposure. Officials say they will continue monitoring water samples in impacted areas as they work to determine the full scope of the problem.Casian urged the utility to stay consistent in its follow-through."Keep up with the recurring tests, because these are people's homes," Casian said. "We can't do without water.”This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Two men were arrested following a nearly monthlong investigation into a string of car burglaries across neighborhoods in Martin County. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office announced the arrests of Stephen Ivan Morris and Shaun Alexander Bilbrey. Both face 36 charges of grand theft, armed burglary, larceny and traveling to commit a burglary. Both were booked into the Martin County Jail on Tuesday. "This probably started with a handful of a few mistakes, and then it escalated rapidly. These kids are in real trouble. They've done a lot of damage in a short period of time, in a one month period of time. For here and now, they've ruined their current life, and they've ruined it for the next couple years as they go through the court system and the prison system, probably," said John Budensiek, Martin Co. See also: Dolly Parton's legacy lives on in Palm Beach County through Imagination Library The investigation into burglaries affecting multiple neighborhoods, including gated communities, began in early August. With assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office SWAT team and Criminal Investigations Division, Martin County detectives served warrants at the St. Lucie County homes of Morris, 19, and Bilbrey, 19. "None of these were scenarios where they forced their way into the cars. They were simply pulling on door handles and grabbing what was easy to get," Budensiek said. The two men allegedly committed 15 burglaries and stole at least 7 firearms. They also allegedly committed a burglary when they went into an open garage and stole a golf cart and drove it around the neighborhood to commit car burglaries. The car burglaries happened in Hobe Sound, Palm City and two areas in Stuart, including the Stuart Yacht and Country Club. Sheriff Budensiek says the two men may have committed other car burglaries too, that have not been reported yet because the victims are unaware their cars were burglarized. "We have one firearm that was stolen in Hobe Sound, and then traded, according to these young men at a gas station for some cash or some kind of a transaction, and we don't know where that is. If you're the one that has that firearm, we want you to know that it's stolen. You won't be in trouble if you bring it back to us. But if we catch you with it, that'll be a whole different ball game," Budensiek explained. The Sheriff says he has a message for firearm owners. "If you're going to keep a firearm in a car, which is not a good idea to start with, lock your car," he said.

Two 19-year-olds from Port St. Lucie were arrested after investigators connected them to 15 burglaries and a string of gun thefts across Martin County. The Martin County Sheriff's Office identified the suspects as Stephen Morris and Shaun Bilbrey. Investigators said the burglaries began on Aug. 1 in Hobe Sound, with the teens traveling by motorcycle and looking for unlocked vehicles across the county. The thefts stretched from Hobe Sound, Palm City and Stuart, hitting a mix of gated and open communities. "It was a combination of gated communities and just communities that you could access by going down the road," Budensiek said. At the Stuart Yacht and Country Club, investigators said the teens went over a wall and stole a golf cart from a resident's garage. Surveillance video from the sheriff's office shows one of the suspects going through a car at the club. When investigators searched the suspects' homes, they found seven stolen guns — five tied to the 15 burglaries. The origin of the remaining two guns has not been determined. Repeated flooding on Ocean Drive in Vero Beach is raising concerns among business owners, and the city says a permanent fix could cost millions of dollars and take years to complete.Lee Olsen, general manager at Waldo's Restaurant and Bar, sent WPTV a video of the flooding on Ocean Drive after Wednesday's storm. He said it was among the worst he has seen.WATCH BELOW: Flooding on Ocean Drive leaves businesses struggling "I've been here 20 years," Olsen said. "Probably one of the worst floodings I've seen."Olsen said the water level was high."When I walked out into the middle of the street, the water was up to my knees," he said.Wednesday was not the first time this week the road flooded."We had the same thing happen on Monday," Olsen said.Olsen said the flooding has become a recurring problem tied to the area's daily weather pattern."Every afternoon we get a thunderstorm. Every afternoon we possibly will end up dealing with flooding," Olsen said.The flooding has also created dangerous conditions for Olsen and his staff after their shifts."I drove down Ocean Drive yesterday to get my employee to their car because the water was so deep; I almost lost my car," Olsen said.Across the street, Aubrey Moxley and Leah Trodglen work at Allure Gallery. Moxley said the flooding builds quickly."It doesn't matter how long it rains for; that water is collecting," Moxley said. "This entire street flooded in less than 30 minutes of rain."Moxley said the flooding is a threat to businesses along the strip."They can't go to the beach, they can't come and shop," Moxley said. "It definitely can be crippling for businesses on Ocean Drive."Moxley said the severity is new."I have never seen the street flood the way that it has been this past week," she said.Olsen said he is worried about what a major storm could bring."These ground-level businesses would end up being flooded, and that's unacceptable," Olsen said. "It needs to be addressed by the city."WPTV reached out to the City of Vero Beach Public Works Department for answers. Staff said the pump stations and other drainage infrastructure were working but are only designed to handle 1 inch of rainfall per hour. The most recent storms exceeded that, delivering 2 or more inches of rainfall in an hour.To fix the flooding, staff said it would require rebuilding the road and making drainage improvements — a project that could cost millions of dollars and take years to complete.Olsen acknowledged the scale of the challenge."It's a big financial endeavor," Olsen said. "Where do you say too much money versus damage to local businesses?"Public works staff said there is no improvement project planned for Ocean Drive at this time.

Gail Giustino, the Stuart woman accused of hoarding more than 100 animals inside her home, pleaded no contest Tuesday to two misdemeanor animal-cruelty-related charges and was sentenced to two years of probation. As part of her sentence, Giustino must undergo a mental health evaluation and have no contact with animals of any species. She will not serve jail time. Giustino, 77, was arrested July 20 after Martin County sheriff’s deputies, Animal Services and Fire Rescue crews executed a search warrant at her Southwest Meadowlark Circle home. Sheriff John Budensiek called it the worst animal hoarding case he had seen in Martin County. She was charged with animal cruelty and confining an animal without sufficient food or water. Investigators said Giustino, a U.S. Postal Service letter carrier, had collected cats she encountered along her mail route. Authorities initially removed 80 cats and 12 dogs. As more animals were captured after the search, the count rose to 100 animals 83 cats and 17 dogs. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast later received 97 cats and 21 dogs from Giustino’s home, operations director Lori Tucker told CBS12 News on Tuesday. All of the dogs from the case have now been adopted, Tucker said. Ten cats remain available for adoption. See also: 2 arrested in string of firearm burglaries across Martin and St. Lucie counties Investigators said the animals were living without adequate food, water, ventilation or air conditioning, and that portions of the home contained several inches of animal waste. A HAZMAT team was called to ventilate the home as crews removed animals, according to the sheriff’s office. Several animals were found to have microchips, leading to reunions with owners who had been searching for missing pets.

"Some of these buildings and some of the facilities have a different you know sort of value from a repurposing perspective."Krasnow said some buildings, like Rosewood Magnet School, could be transformed."It's everything from repurposing medical office to quasi-flex space," Krasnow said.Krasnow said larger schools and properties could be redeveloped."[It] will look more like commercial, maybe some retail out along the front, and then some residential in the back," Krasnow said.Dodds said the district will reexamine interest in the properties and whether they need to be sold around December or January. A 16-year-old girl died after she fell through a hole in the roof of an abandoned four-story building last Saturday in Sebastian, deputies said.According to a new release from the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, deputies and fire rescue personnel responded to 9846 Riverside Preserve Drive in Sebastian at about 10:35 p.m. after receiving a 911 call reporting that the girl had fallen from a concrete structure and was critically injured. WATCH: 911 CALLS RELEASED AFTER TEEN FALLS IN ABANDONED BUILDING Deputies arrived and found a group of minors along with the critically injured teen on the second floor of the abandoned building. "The investigation determined the group had been trespassing on the property and was on the roof when the teen fell through a hole in the roof, dropping approximately 29 feet to the floor below," the sheriff's office said. The sheriff's office said one of the minors in the group knew CPR and immediately began life-saving measures. Newly released 911 calls capture the frantic moments after the fall. "Okay, what is going on?" the dispatcher asked."A girl fell from about three stories tall in the abandoned condos through a hole," the caller said.When the dispatcher asked if the teen was awake, the caller said she was not but still had a pulse. "Is she breathing though?" the dispatcher asked."Um, no," the caller said."Okay, we need to begin CPR," the dispatcher said.The sheriff's office said one of the minors in the group knew CPR and immediately began life-saving measures. The 911 calls reveal dispatchers guided the teens through the process, counting compressions in real time."Keep going. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5," the dispatcher said.As the teens waited for help to arrive, a dispatcher reassured them."They're coming as fast as they can," the dispatcher said."Okay, okay," the caller responded.The 16-year-old was flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where she died from her injuries a short time later. Detectives are actively investigating the teen's death, but said, "At this time, all evidence indicates this was an accident." Nearby residents are calling for the buildings to be condemned following the tragedy. The victim's name has not been released. "The Indian River County Sheriff's Office extends its deepest sympathies to the family during this difficult time. We also want to remind the public, especially parents and teens, of the serious dangers posed by climbing on abandoned structures, and the legal consequences of trespassing on privately owned property," the sheriff's office said.

Lucie Police Department officers have been placed on paid administrative leave as investigations continue into two separate incidents involving political campaign signs that occurred last week on Southwest Airoso Boulevard.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: 'I'm disappointed that she doesn't take accountability for her and her husband's actions,' Candidate Steven Giordano tells WPTV's Tyler HatfieldThe officers placed on leave effective Tuesday, are Lieutenant Aaron Martin, Lieutenant Jason Vega and Detective Sergeant Joseph Alves. Chief Leo Niemczyk made the decision following a review of the initial facts and timeline surrounding the incidents. Lucie Police Department released more information regarding the incidents over the weekend.The first incident occurred on Aug. 5 near the intersection of SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thanksgiving Avenue.A Port St. Lucie Police sergeant observed Steven Giordano and an unidentified adult female near political campaign signs at a residence and initiated an investigation after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard.Detectives reviewed surveillance video from the area, which appears to show Giordano and the unidentified adult female arrive at the residence, approach campaign signs displayed in the yard, and interact with the signage. The video further appears to show the unidentified female remove a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before a different campaign sign was placed in the yard.WATCH BELOW: WPTV's Tyler Hatfield speaks with Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin after husband placed on administrative leaveDetectives collected the video evidence and are evaluating it alongside statements, physical evidence, and all other information gathered during the investigation.Officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement, and authorization of the campaign signs, including whether the movement or replacement of the signs was authorized by the property owner at the time the incident occurred.The second incident occurred on Aug. 7 near SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, where officers responded to a disturbance involving political campaign signs.During the investigation, officers learned that Lt. Aaron Martin and Steven Giordano were involved in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of campaign signs at a nearby residence.Officers reviewed video recordings provided by the involved parties, which depict Aaron Martin and Giordano engaged in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of political campaign signs at the residence.Investigators interviewed the homeowners and learned that both residents believed they had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property. Officers determined that one homeowner communicated permission for one campaign's sign, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, separately conveyed permission to individuals associated with the opposing campaign.Investigators believe the language barrier contributed to a misunderstanding regarding which campaign signs were authorized to be displayed and whether previously placed signs could be moved or replaced.WATCH PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: Port St. Lucie police release details on 2 separate political campaign sign investigationsThe Port St. Lucie Police Department says it remains committed to ensuring all investigations are conducted fairly and impartially, maintaining its longstanding commitment to integrity, professionalism and accountability.Lt. Aaron Martin's wife is Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin, who is currently running for re-election.WPTV's Tyler Hatfield spoke with the mayor on Thursday, following the news that her husband is on paid administrative leave with the Port St. Lucie Police Department following the investigation."Whenever there's a criminal investigation of any kind, it's standard operating procedure for the police department to place people on administrative leave pending the outcome of an investigation," she said.She said she hopes the incident will not impact her campaign and Tuesday's primary election."This issue about signage and campaign signs has nothing to do with my campaign in terms of how I have been leading the city and how I will continue to lead the city and the important issues that we're facing here in Port St. Lucie," Mayor Shannon Martin said.When asked what she wanted to tell voters learning about her husband's leave in real time, the mayor pushed back on the framing of the situation."It was blown way out of proportion, but the process has to work the way that the process has to work in order to ensure fairness and transparency," she said. "So that process will go forward, but that has nothing to do with the elections. It has nothing to do with my campaign, whatsoever."The mayor said she intends to press forward despite the circumstances."It's a disappointing situation. However, I'm going to continue to move forward and making sure that I am continuing my campaign. And continuing to work to earn residents' votes," Shannon Martin said.When asked to comment on the investigation itself, the mayor declined."I cannot comment on that. It has nothing to do with me. I'm not part of that process whatsoever. I've never been part of that process as a mayor. That is not my role, and it will never be part of part of my process," she said.

Thirty-six dogs are now safe and beginning a long road to recovery after being rescued from what officials are calling a "house of horror" in Palm City. The animals were discovered living in filth, covered in matted fur and their own feces. According to officials, the condition of the dogs was shocking."We're averaging about six pounds of mat per dog," one staff member said.Crews performing emergency grooming have found 4-inch shards of glass and metal hidden in the dense, matted fur. The shelter is using every available space to house and treat the animals, with 20 of the 36 dogs having been groomed so far.The severity of the situation drew a swift response from local leaders. State Representatives Meg Weinberger and John Snyder, State Senator Gayle Harrell, and Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek toured the facility to see the dogs' condition firsthand."It's time to really roll up our sleeves, get up to Tallahassee this session, and to try and make sure we're doing everything we can to make sure this never happens again," Rep. Snyder said."We need to work with our sheriffs in particular to really gain that experience as to what they are seeing out there," said Senator Harrell. "We need to empower our sheriffs to be able to take the steps that they are that they need to take from our conversations today. We need to empower them to do what's necessary to protect the animals."Rep. Weinberger added, "Sadly, I've seen cases like this, but this was really bad... the fact that nobody could get in to check on these dogs, it was horrific."The officials agreed that current laws are not enough. The City of Stuart has been awarded $79 million in federal funding to replace the aging St. Lucie River Railroad Bridge as part of a massive $5.3 billion nationwide investment in rail safety and infrastructure announced by U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy on Tuesday.The grant, part of the National Railroad Partnership Program, will fund the replacement of the 100-year-old single-track bridge with a modern double-track structure featuring dramatically improved clearances for boats and vessels navigating the Okeechobee Waterway. Florida received a total of $496 million from the program, with the Stuart bridge project representing the second-largest allocation in the state.The new bridge will increase horizontal clearance from 50 feet to approximately 90 feet, while vertical clearance will jump from just 6.5 feet to 17.75 feet when in the closed position. These improvements will allow more than 90% of vessels to pass without requiring the bridge to open, significantly reducing delays for marine traffic on the federal navigation channel."Anyone who's spent time on the St. Lucie River knows that century-old bridge is too low, sitting at 6 feet, too narrow, and stuck in the closed position more often than it should be," said Congressman Brian Mast. "It's a daily headache for boaters and a safety risk for everyone who shares that corridor."The bridge serves both Brightline passenger trains and Florida East Coast Railway freight operations, making it a critical piece of infrastructure for the region's transportation network. The replacement project is expected to improve safety, reduce vehicle collisions at grade crossings, and encourage more people to use passenger rail instead of driving.The Stuart project is part of what the Trump administration is calling the "Golden Age of Rail," with the $5.3 billion investment targeting rail safety upgrades nationwide. The funding will improve over 1,000 grade crossings across the country and close more than 30 dangerous crossings. Grade crossings are the second leading cause of rail-related deaths in the United States, with more than 2,000 incidents and 200 fatalities occurring annually at these intersections.Other Florida projects receiving funding include $356 million for the Florida Department of Transportation to upgrade up to 910 highway-rail grade crossings statewide, $57 million for a new Brightline station in Cocoa, and $4 million for Jacksonville's Amtrak station relocation project.The total cost of the Stuart bridge replacement is estimated at $262 million. Combined with a previous $130 million federal grant awarded in 2023, the project now has approximately $209 million in federal funding committed.Construction timelines and additional project details have not yet been announced by the City of Stuart.

Florida voters now have another way to crunch the numbers on Amendment 3, though the math still comes with plenty of political variables.Florida TaxWatch, the nonpartisan watchdog behind Florida’s annual “Budget Turkey” list, launched a new online resource center Friday designed to explain the sweeping property-tax proposal before the November election.Watch report from Forrest Saunders“With Amendment 3 on the November ballot, there is much discussion and confusion related to this proposed property-tax measure,” Florida TaxWatch Chair David Casey said.The Florida Property Tax Resource Center includes an interactive county map, local millage rates, frequently asked questions and estimates showing how much revenue local governments could lose if the amendment passes.Think less crystal ball, more fiscal X-ray.“This amendment would cut property tax locally by an estimated $45.8 billion over five years,” Florida TaxWatch President and CEO Jeff Kottkamp said.What Amendment 3 would changeAmendment 3 would expand Florida’s homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. School property taxes would remain unchanged.The proposal would also reduce the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%. That category includes rental homes, second homes and commercial properties.The measure must receive at least 60% support from voters to become part of the Florida Constitution.TaxWatch has not yet taken an official position on the amendment. Kottkamp said the organization will announce its recommendation in a broader constitutional amendment guide expected next month.No personalized estimateOne feature missing from the new resource center is a calculator showing how much an individual homeowner could save.TaxWatch said such a figure would be too speculative because cities and counties could respond to the revenue loss by cutting services, increasing millage rates or imposing new fees and special assessments.However, a private calculator we previously featured allows homeowners to enter their taxable value and local millage rates to generate an estimate.The tool was created by Casey Vockell of My Exemption Check.“The impact to the local taxing authorities is going to be bad, but the benefit to the taxpayer is not going to be nearly as big as one might think,” Vockell said.In one example, the calculator found that a Hillsborough County home assessed at $500,000 could save less than $209 per month by 2028.The estimate does not account for any later decisions by local governments that could reduce or offset those savings.Opponents warn of service cutsThe amendment’s critics argue the proposal would shift costs rather than eliminate them, potentially forcing communities to reduce spending on police, firefighters, emergency medical services, libraries and other local programs.“The language on voters’ ballots may have changed, but that doesn’t change the fact that Amendment 3 is still a scam and a tax shift,” said Jackson Peel with Save Our Services. “That’s either going to raise our costs or take away services that Floridians rely on every day.”The ballot summary was recently rewritten after a Leon County judge found the Legislature’s original wording biased and misleading. The ruling did not remove the amendment from the ballot.DeSantis promises help for rural countiesSupporters, including Gov. Ron DeSantis, argue local governments can absorb the reductions by trimming spending. DeSantis has also promised state assistance for rural and fiscally constrained counties.If the amendment passes, DeSantis said lawmakers would need to return to Tallahassee for a special session to implement it. That would leave a short window before he leaves office in January.“I’d hate for people to deprive themselves of a really significant tax break because you think somehow they’re not going to have money to have a police force or something,” DeSantis said.Despite the governor’s backing, passage is not guaranteed. Amendment 3 must clear Florida’s 60% constitutional threshold in November.For voters, the new TaxWatch center supplies more numbers. The central question remains the same: How much stays in homeowners’ wallets, and what might disappear from their communities?

Tourism this year in Florida is showing some declines, and one of the biggest drops is with Canadian tourists.The data from Visit Florida shows 721,000 Canadian visitors in the 2nd quarter of 2026, a drop of 4.2% from the 2nd quarter in 2025.For 2026 so far, 1.6 million Canadian tourists is a drop of 13.9% over the same period in 2025.WATCH: Canadian tourist numbers decline in FloridaOverall, the state for the first six months of this year had 73.5 million visitors, a number that is a decline of 1.4% from a year ago.Inflation, gas prices and a chilly winter in Florida certainly have an impact, but the larger Canadian tourist declines seem to indicate something else."Not trusting, 100 percent," says Emily Gasle, a college student studying in Montreal and visiting Delray Beach. "I feel like because of the tariffs and recent news, obviously there's more of negative feelings."Managers in businesses along Atlantic Avenue say the declines in Canadians seem soft so far."In general, our tourism is mostly Canadian, northeastern," says Benny Magro at Sandwiches By The Sea. "I've been managing businesses in this area for a long time, and we have to adjust."

hero.headline: Martin County Sheriff warns residents less safe after state orders license plate reader removal
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Transportation ordered local agencies on Monday to remove license plate readers from state highways within 30 days, prompting Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek to warn Tuesday that the decision makes county residents fundamentally less safe. The memorandum came after Gov. Ron DeSantis publicly called the technology out of control last week.

Budensiek pointed to several major arrests made with help from the cameras, including the arrest of former President Donald Trump's would-be assassin, the rescue of two young girls headed to Nebraska with a kidnapper last year, and the arrest of a traveling rooftop burglary crew. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers praised license plate readers like Flock cameras after they aided in a homicide arrest last month. Flowers said a murderer was caught and taken off the streets because of the Flock system.

Port St. Lucie police is pausing the use of license plate readers in the city. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office will limit license plate reader use to investigations involving forcible felonies and missing or endangered persons. Former Martin County Sheriff William Snyder called for meaningful legislation that regulates camera use and protects privacy while allowing the community to keep the cameras and remain safe.

Budensiek proposed limiting camera use to criminal investigations and missing persons cases, requiring a case number and report for public record. He said he would support a public professional auditing system if people still do not trust law enforcement. Stuart resident Sean Reilly said he has never supported the cameras because he considers them an invasion of privacy. Neighbor Brandee Bailey said license plate readers play an important role in keeping the community safe, while neighbor Kristina Ramsey said the cameras have helped catch a lot of criminals.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Police pause Flock camera use after state revokes road permits
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department announced an operational pause on all Automated License Plate Reader technology, widely recognized as Flock cameras, following a Florida Department of Transportation memorandum revoking permits for ALPR systems on state roads. The pause took effect Wednesday.

During the pause, PSLPD says ALPR access will be limited exclusively to exigent circumstances regarding immediate threat to human life, or in circumstances in which access to ALPR information may help prevent the loss of life or threat to great bodily harm.

Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the decision reflects a balance between technology that has proven an important tool for officers and investigators and the responsibility to listen to the community and respect state direction. He said the department has a responsibility to ensure its policies reflect the highest standards of trust, accountability, and public safety.

PSLPD says it will continue to monitor developments at the state level and review any additional guidance as it becomes available. The cameras have helped the department protect people and solve crimes, according to the chief.

cards.headline: Data center proposed for 174 acres in western St. Lucie County near Interstate 95
cards.teaser: Willow Lakes LLC submitted a rezoning application in June to St. Lucie County to change 174 acres of its 203-acre property off West Midway Road and Interstate 95 to light industrial use to allow for a data center.
cards.body:
Willow Lakes LLC submitted a rezoning application in June to St. Lucie County to change 174 acres of its 203-acre property off West Midway Road and Interstate 95 to light industrial use to allow for a data center. The rezoning application said the applicant intends to develop a data center on the portion of the property to be zoned Light Industrial. The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community, with developer Devcon Enterprises.

Attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project. Dobbins said the landowner believes the property is well-suited for a data center, citing existing Florida Power Light transmission lines on the site and a man-made lake that could be used for a closed-loop cooling system. The applicant requests the remaining 26 acres to be zoned general commercial, intended for development for commercial retail uses, and could include a hotel, gas station and restaurants or fast food.

Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the proposal could be an appropriate use of the land, but he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption and no noise pollution. Parker Whiteside, who lives about a mile and a half from the property, said she values the quiet, open character of the area and opposes the idea. The application is scheduled to go before the Planning and Zoning Board in September.

When asked about the potential data center, her reaction was immediate. "I hate that idea," Whiteside said. The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community, with developer Devcon Enterprises. Attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project. "He was looking at what else he could potentially do at the property," Dobbins said. Dobbins said the landowner believes the property is well-suited for a data center, citing existing Florida Power Light transmission lines on the site and a man-made lake that could be used for a closed-loop cooling system. According to the rezoning application, the applicant requests the remaining 26 acres to be zoned general commercial, "intended for development for commercial retail uses, and could include a hotel, gas station and/or restaurants/fast food." Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the proposal could be an appropriate use of the land, but he has conditions. "Data centers are kind of the rage right now," Broderick said. Broderick said he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption and no noise pollution. "If they don't, then I will not be supportive of it," Broderick said. The rezoning application said that if rezoning is approved, the applicant intends to enter into an agreement with a partner company which would develop the data center. cards.headline: Body found in Hutchinson Island mangroves believed to be missing Oklahoma visitor
cards.teaser: A body discovered in mangroves near the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island is believed to belong to Michael Anthony Debevec II, an Oklahoma visitor who was reported missing after last being seen at Chastain Beach on Aug. 26.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office is investigating a body found in the mangroves just north of the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island that is believed to belong to Michael Anthony Debevec II, an Oklahoma visitor who was reported missing after last being seen at Chastain Beach on Aug. 26. Investigators are waiting for a positive identification, but Sheriff John Budensiek said he believes the body belongs to Debevec because the clothing matches what Debevec was last seen wearing in surveillance video.

Debevec's family filed a missing person report on Saturday after a good Samaritan found his wallet on the beach near the House of Refuge. Deputies later discovered Debevec's car parked at Chastain Beach. The Sheriff's Office then searched the area of Hutchinson Island by land, sea and air.

The search continued through Tuesday morning when deputies found Debevec's backpack hanging high in a tree. As they continued through the thick mangroves and brushed sea grapes, they located the deceased body. The body was found heavily decomposed.

The Medical Examiner's Office is working to determine the exact cause of death, looking for signs of trauma and performing a toxicology report. Debevec's family says he has gone missing before and has a history of substance abuse, but says he had gotten clean.

hero.headline: Speeding driver crashes into two parked trucks on SW Lucero Drive in Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
A speeding driver crashed into two parked trucks on Southwest Lucero Drive in Port St. Lucie around 3:40 p.m., causing extensive damage and renewing resident concerns about chronic speeding on the residential road. Security video recorded the crash, which shows a black truck traveling at a high rate of speed before going off the road into the grass and slamming into the two parked trucks.

The driver of the black truck sustained only minor injuries, Port St. Lucie police said. The two parked trucks, both owned by Rocky Burkhead and essential to his pressure washing business, sustained extensive damage. Burkhead said he had to rent a U-Haul to continue working.

Neighbors said the crash highlights a persistent speeding problem on Southwest Lucero Drive, where the speed limit is 25 mph but drivers rarely adhere to it. Courtney Gray said people fly by on the road all the time. The lack of sidewalks compounds the danger for residents who walk along the road with children and pets. Gray said she walks every day with her baby in a stroller and was thankful she was not home when the crash happened.

Burkhead suggested Port St. Lucie police station officers in the area and issue heavy fines to address the speeding. Gray said speed bumps may be needed to prevent similar crashes. Port St. Lucie police have not responded to inquiries about arrests related to the crash or the possibility of speed bumps or additional patrols.

"When I heard the crash, I thought it was thunder," Elaine Harmon, a neighbor, said. "I heard a loud explosion," said another neighbor, Rocky Burkhead. "Thought it was just lightning like we've been having over the last few days." But when Burkhead stepped outside, he realized the situation was far worse than a weather-related incident. "I had no idea what to think. I was just at a loss for words. My first concern was, 'Is he OK?'" Burkhead said. Lucie police said the man in the black truck sustained only minor injuries. However, Burkhead said the damage to the two parked trucks hit in the collision was extensive. Both trucks belong to Burkhead and are essential for his pressure washing business. I had to rent a U-Haul today. You're limited on what you can do, how far you can go," Burkhead said. Neighbors said the crash is the most dramatic example of speeding on Southwest Lucero Drive but emphasized it is not an isolated incident. The speed limit on the road is 25 mph, but residents said drivers rarely adhere to it. "People do fly by on this road all the time," Courtney Gray, a neighbor, said. "There's a big problem with speeding on this road," Burkhead said. Residents are particularly concerned because the road lacks sidewalks, yet many people walk along it with children and pets. "I walk every day with (my baby) in the stroller or whatever. I'm just so thankful we weren't home when it happened," Gray said. "I think what they need to do is put some officers in the area, pull a few people over with some heavy-duty fines," Burkhead said. "Seems like something like this is going to keep happening if we don't have speed bumps," Gray said. Lucie police have not yet responded to inquiries about arrests related to the crash or the possibility of speed bumps or additional patrols. hero.headline: Motorcycle crash shuts down I-95 Southbound in Martin County near Hobe Sound
hero.body:
A motorcycle crash shut down I-95 Southbound in southern Martin County on Tuesday, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office and Florida Highway Patrol. The crash took place around mile marker 98, just north of Hobe Sound and Exit 96 at Bridge Road, and south of Exit 101 at Kanner Highway in Stuart.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office said southbound lanes were completely shut down following the crash. The driver of the motorcycle was flown to a nearby hospital. Florida Highway Patrol remained on the scene investigating.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office advised drivers traveling southbound to avoid the area and expect significant delays. The crash occurred in the area between two major exits serving Hobe Sound and Stuart.

Florida Highway Patrol was conducting the investigation at the scene. The crash location at mile marker 98 placed it in the southern portion of Martin County along the major interstate corridor.

cards.headline: Tiger Woods change-of-plea hearing set for Wednesday in Martin County DUI case
cards.teaser: Tiger Woods is scheduled for a change-of-plea hearing Wednesday in Martin County, months after his Jupiter Island DUI arrest.
cards.body:
Tiger Woods is set for a change-of-plea hearing Wednesday, September 2, in Martin County, months after his Jupiter Island DUI arrest. Woods was arrested in March on Jupiter Island for DUI. Deputies said they believe he was under the influence of something other than alcohol. Woods pleaded not guilty at the time.

In June, prosecutors were granted access to Woods' medical records from the day of his arrest. The order stated that prosecutors can review records from Woods' hospital visit. The sheriff's office previously said Woods was briefly taken to a hospital to be cleared before being taken to jail. The order specifies that the records will be disclosed only to the state, designated law enforcement officers or experts, and the defense. Prosecutors have also subpoenaed Woods' prescription records.

cards.headline: Two people, dog escape Jensen Beach garage fire caused by charging lithium-ion battery
cards.teaser: Two people and a dog safely escaped a garage fire Monday morning in Jensen Beach after a charging lithium-ion battery burst into flames.
cards.body:
Two people and a dog safely escaped a garage fire Monday morning in Jensen Beach after firefighters quickly contained the blaze, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The fire was reported just after 6:30 a.m. in the 2700 block of Northeast Cypress Lane. When crews arrived, they found heavy smoke coming from the garage of the home.

According to the homeowner, a lithium-ion battery had been charging in the garage before the fire started. Firefighters immediately evacuated the residence and worked to contain the flames, preventing the fire from spreading beyond the garage. Officials said crews successfully extinguished the fire, and no neighboring structures were threatened.

Fire rescue officials called the incident a close call and are reminding residents to follow proper lithium-ion battery safety practices. They encourage people to unplug batteries once they are fully charged to help prevent overheating and potential fires. For additional information on lithium-ion battery safety, residents can visit the National Fire Protection Association's website.

cards.headline: Body found in Hutchinson Island mangroves believed to be missing Oklahoma visitor
cards.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office is investigating a body found in the mangroves near the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island. Investigators believe the body belongs to Michael Anthony Debevec II, who was reported missing after visiting Chastain Beach.
cards.body:
A body discovered in the mangroves on Hutchinson Island is believed to belong to Michael Anthony Debevec II, an Oklahoma visitor who was reported missing after last being seen on August 26 at Chastain Beach, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The body was found just north of the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island on Tuesday.

Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the clothing on the heavily decomposed body matched what Debevec was last seen wearing in surveillance video. Debevec's family filed a missing person's report on Saturday after a good Samaritan found his wallet on the beach near the House of Refuge. Deputies later discovered Debevec's car parked at Chastain Beach.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office searched the area by land, sea and air. Deputies found Debevec's backpack hanging high in a tree south of the House of Refuge before locating the deceased body in thick mangroves and sea grapes. The Medical Examiner's Office is working to determine the exact cause of death and performing a toxicology report. Debevec's family said he had a history of substance abuse but had gotten clean.

hero.headline: Body found in Martin County mangroves believed to be missing Port St. Lucie man
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office recovered a body Tuesday from deep within the mangroves near the House of Refuge following an extensive search for a missing Port St. Lucie man. Sheriff John Budensiek said investigators had not officially confirmed the identity, but the deceased person was wearing clothing matching what Michael Anthony Debevec was believed to have been wearing. Budensiek said a Good Samaritan found a wallet Saturday belonging to Debevec and went to his home to return it, which led the family to file a missing person report. Investigators found Debevec's vehicle Saturday afternoon at Chastain Beach, a little more than two miles from where the body was discovered.

Investigators determined that Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. on August 27 and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed that his phone was in use Friday morning and moving back and forth between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge. The discovery of the wallet and vehicle prompted detectives and ground and aerial units to launch an extensive search.

On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body. Budensiek said there was a lot of decomposition, making it impossible to determine cause of death.

Debevec's family was notified that a body was found. Budensiek said investigators believe they found Debevec but could not confirm whether it was him.

hero.headline: Body found in Martin County mangroves believed to be missing Port St. Lucie man
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office recovered a body Tuesday morning from deep within the mangroves near the House of Refuge, believed to be that of Michael Anthony Debevec, a Port St. Lucie man reported missing Aug. 27. Sheriff John Budensiek said investigators had not officially confirmed the identity because of extensive decomposition, but the deceased person was wearing clothing matching what Debevec was believed to have been wearing. The sheriff said it was impossible to determine cause of death.

A Good Samaritan found a wallet Saturday belonging to Debevec and went to his home to return it, which led his family to file a missing person report. Investigators found Debevec's vehicle Saturday afternoon at Chastain Beach, a little more than two miles from where the body was discovered. The discovery of the wallet and vehicle prompted detectives and ground and aerial units to launch an extensive search.

Investigators determined that Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. Aug. 27 and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed that his phone was in use Friday morning and moving back and forth between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge.

On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body. Debevec's family was notified that a body was found.

hero.headline: Florida orders removal of automated license plate readers from state highways within 30 days
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Transportation is ordering local agencies to remove automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras, from state highways within 30 days. The department cited concerns over rapid expansion, data privacy, misuse and surveillance schemes in announcing the directive.

The announcement follows public statements by Gov. Ron DeSantis, who called the technology out of control days earlier and raised concerns about Florida becoming a surveillance state. More than 8,000 Flock cameras are documented across Florida, according to state records. The decision affects cameras operated by local law enforcement agencies and municipalities that have installed the devices on state-controlled roadways.

Palm Beach County residents expressed divided opinions on the order. Reid Mollway said the level of data collection represents an invasion of privacy, noting that tracking data is not fully clarified and is kept for dates that have no expiration. David Vega and other residents defended the cameras as serving an important public safety purpose. Vega said the cameras allow people to walk streets and use highways more safely.

Nikki Fried, chair of the Florida Democratic Party, criticized Republicans for allowing the unchecked spread of the technology across the state. Multiple local law enforcement agencies have been contacted for comment but have not yet responded to the state order.

hero.headline: Indian River County Sheriff's Office employee dies in Brevard County vehicle crash
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that Civilian Corrections Assistant Cassi Taylor died in a vehicle crash in Brevard County. Taylor joined the Indian River County Sheriff's Office on July 20, 2026, and was scheduled to be officially sworn in on Monday, Aug. 31.

Taylor is the daughter of Deputy Scott Burke, whom the Sheriff's Office said many in the community may know from community events. The Sheriff's Office released a statement asking the community to keep Burke and the entire family in their prayers.

The Sheriff's Office did not release additional details about the crash. Taylor had been with the agency for just over a month before her death.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office is mourning the loss of the civilian corrections assistant, who had not yet completed her official swearing-in ceremony before the fatal crash occurred in neighboring Brevard County.
