cards.headline: Corgi found three streets away after EF0 tornado in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: Luna, a 6-year-old corgi, went missing after an EF0 tornado struck the Bay St. Lucie community and pushed open owner Molly Wing-Berman's front door.
cards.body:
Luna, a 6-year-old corgi, is back safe with her owner after going missing when an EF0 tornado struck the Bay St. Lucie community in Port St. Lucie. The force of the tornado pushed open Molly Wing-Berman's front door, made a big hole in the wall, took all the mail and items from surfaces, went out the locked back door and put the items in the pool. Neighbors eventually found Luna three streets away.

As the tornado approached, Berman had already gone to her laundry room for safety with her 2-year-old rescue dog, Enzo. Berman said she was in a panic and looked for Luna everywhere with her daughter, searching all over the house and yard. When Luna was found, she was shaking all over and has not really left Berman's side since. Luna now has a new nickname: Luna ToTo.

As the tornado approached, Berman had already gone to her laundry room for safety with her 2-year-old rescue dog, Enzo. She tried to bring Luna along, but when the pup did not respond or follow, Berman thought she was in her usual hiding spot under the bed. “I was in a panic,” Berman said. “We looked for her everywhere. My daughter came over, and we looked all over the house for her. We looked all over the yard for her.” Neighbors eventually found Luna three streets away. “She was shaking all over and hasn’t really left my side since,” Berman said. It’s unclear whether Luna, like other items in Berman’s home, was picked up by the power of the tornado or if she ran out after being spooked by the storm. “She’s been sleeping very close to me.” Luna now has a new nickname: Luna ToTo. hero.headline: Palm City hit-and-run suspect arrested after two-hour manhunt through swamps
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested Likenson Daceus after a two-hour manhunt that ended a quarter mile into Palm City natural lands Wednesday evening. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission alerted the Martin County Sheriff's Office about a man suspected of stealing palmetto berries from the Savannah Preserve. A deputy spotted the suspect's car in Palm City and attempted a traffic stop, but the suspect fled. Daceus then crashed head-on into another vehicle on SW Rivers End Way and Murphy Road, leaving the driver with minor injuries. The police report says he left a juvenile in his car before taking off on foot.

The manhunt involved multiple agencies including MCSO, FWC, and Port St. Lucie. They utilized road patrols, K-9 teams, aviation and drone units. The pursuit led law enforcement through dense brush and swamp conditions. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek described how deputies tracked Daceus through the area. Deputies ran through the neighborhood and several yards. Canine deputies arrived and neighbors pointed to the last location they saw him running. Deputies picked up a track, found his hat, and tracked him through dense woods, through a backyard, and into the swamp.

Neighbors near the Wind Stone community said the heavy police presence caught them by surprise. Resident Tanya Talanczuck said she sheltered in place during the search. She closed her doors and said she did not want him in her house. Talanczuck described the Wind Stone community as a very safe neighborhood.

Daceus is charged with one felony and a misdemeanor for fleeing with disregard for safety and resisting arrest. Budensiek said once Daceus hurt one of their people, it was game on for the sheriff's office. He said he truly believed Daceus would have done anything to get away and felt he was a danger to the community. Budensiek said deputies are not afraid of snakes, alligators, swamps, oceans, or sharks because they are from here.

hero.headline: New College of Florida spent $800,000 on outside PR consultants despite 13-member in-house communications team
hero.body:
New College of Florida has paid approximately $800,000 to two outside public relations consultants since 2023, both hired through no-bid contracts, even as the school maintains a 13-member in-house marketing and communications team, public records show. The spending comes as Gov. Ron DeSantis has defended more than $60 million in state funding to transform the small liberal arts college of about 1,000 students away from what he calls woke indoctrination.

More than $400,000 has gone to TMF Communications, run by Taryn Fenske, a former spokesperson for both New College President Richard Corcoran during his time as Florida's education commissioner and for Governor DeSantis. Fenske also led DeSantis' presidential super PAC before securing her no-bid contract with New College in July 2023. According to college invoices, Fenske has been paid upwards of $15,000 per month, plus travel expenses, to help improve the school's brand, create proactive messaging, and produce promotional videos. Another nearly $400,000 has gone to Evandr.co, a company run by Katy Saeger, a California PR consultant who describes her crisis communication services as behind the scenes and discreet. Her no-bid contract with New College, signed in November 2023, is worth just over $12,000 per month, plus nearly $30,000 in back pay. This January, Evandr.co's monthly fees were reduced to $5,000.

The spending comes as New College faculty have recently been asked to make budget cuts. A state audit last year found New College, while the smallest public college in Florida's university system, is also the most financially inefficient. It costs nearly three times as much to earn a degree at New College than UF, the state's largest university. Spending per student at New College during FY 2024 was $83,207, nearly double spending at UF and the highest among all public universities in the state.

New College spokesman Jamie Miller defended the outsourced PR hires, saying the school, like many colleges and universities across Florida, works with outside vendors in a variety of operational areas, including communications and marketing. President Corcoran said the consultants were hired when the school's own PR department wasn't fully staffed and the college was facing state and federal investigations. Ben Wilcox, who leads Integrity Florida, a nonpartisan government watchdog group, said the contracts raise concerns for taxpayers. That's pretty much how government operates these days, where we see these kinds of sweetheart deals given to former allies who are being rewarded for their loyalty, Wilcox said.

hero.headline: Vero Beach utility bills to jump nearly $39 per month by 2029 as city approves rate increases
hero.body:
Vero Beach utility customers will face significant bill increases over the next four years after both the city's Utility Commission and City Council unanimously approved a comprehensive rate increase plan to fund major infrastructure improvements. The Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to increase water and sewer rates beginning on Oct. 1. A typical residential customer using 4,000 gallons per month currently pays $83.54 for combined water and sewer service. By 2029, that same bill will reach $122.45 monthly, an increase of nearly $39 per month, or 46.7% over current rates.

The rate increases stem from a $217 million capital improvement program planned through 2030. The centerpiece is a new Water Reclamation Facility currently under construction in Vero Beach. To finance the project, the city plans to issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027. The bonds are structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate, creating average annual debt service of approximately $8.66 million. An additional $42.3 million in grants will also support the project.

Water rates will increase 10% in fiscal year 2027, 7.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 5% in each of the following two years. Wastewater rates face steeper increases at 15% in both fiscal years 2027 and 2028, 10% in 2029, and 5% in 2030. Reclaimed water customers will see the largest percentage increases at 25% in both 2027 and 2028, followed by 5% annual increases. Beyond capital construction, the utility's operating expenses continue climbing at an average annual rate of 4.1%. Operating costs will grow from approximately $25.6 million in fiscal year 2026 to more than $32 million by 2030.

The bond amount represents a significant jump from earlier projections. A 2022 rate study anticipated an $80 million bond issuance, but that figure has grown by $45 million due to cost escalation. The ordinance creates a new Wastewater Readiness-to-Serve Charge affecting property owners who receive city water service but use septic tanks while having public wastewater service available nearby. The charge starts at $40.85 monthly for typical residential customers as of Oct. 1, rising to $54.24 monthly by Oct. Property owners receive 75 days notice before the charge takes effect.

hero.headline: David Jolly calls for reopened Hope Florida investigation after grand jury finds $10 million in taxpayer money misappropriated
hero.body:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly called Thursday for the Hope Florida investigation to be reopened after a newly leaked grand jury report concluded that $10 million in taxpayer money was misappropriated for political purposes. The report, obtained by CBS Miami, details how money from a $67 million Medicaid settlement between Florida and healthcare company Centene moved through Hope Florida and ultimately reached political groups. The grand jury found that $10 million from the settlement went to the Hope Florida Foundation, a program championed by first lady Casey DeSantis that connects people in need with charities, churches, and other community organizations. The decision to send the $10 million to Hope Florida was the original misappropriation, according to the report.

The grand jury traced how the money was then divided into two $5 million grants to separate nonprofits. According to the report, $8.5 million eventually went to Keep Florida Clean, a political committee chaired by James Uthmeier, now the state's Attorney General and then Governor Ron DeSantis' chief of staff. The committee subsequently sent $7 million to the Republican Party of Florida. The grand jury included a flow chart tracing the money from Centene through Hope Florida and the nonprofits into political organizations. While the report says jurors could plainly see taxpayer money was misused for political purposes, the grand jury did not recommend criminal charges. The report says jurors could not prove who made the original decision to send the $10 million to Hope Florida, and no one involved took responsibility for making that decision.

Governor DeSantis strongly disputed the grand jury's conclusions at a press conference Thursday in Lake City. He said no Medicaid money was diverted and argued the $10 million was part of a private contribution tied to the settlement. lead_independence.headline: New College of Florida spends nearly $1 million on outside PR consultants despite 13-member in-house team
lead_independence.lead: New College of Florida has paid approximately $800,000 to two outside public relations consultants since 2023, both hired through no-bid contracts, even as the school maintains a 13-member in-house marketing and communications team, public records show. The spending comes as Governor Ron DeSantis has defended more than $60 million in state funding to transform the small liberal arts college of about 1,000 students away from what he calls woke indoctrination. More than $400,000 has gone to TMF Communications, run by Taryn Fenske, a former spokesperson for both New College President Richard Corcoran during his time as Florida's education commissioner and for Governor DeSantis. Fenske also led DeSantis' presidential super PAC before securing her no-bid contract with New College in July 2023. According to college invoices, Fenske has been paid upwards of $15,000 per month, plus travel expenses, to help improve the school's brand, create proactive messaging, and produce promotional videos.

hero.headline: Vero Beach flooding on Ocean Drive threatens businesses as city says fix could cost millions
hero.body:
Repeated flooding on Ocean Drive in Vero Beach is raising concerns among business owners, and the city says a permanent fix could cost millions of dollars and take years to complete. Wednesday's storm flooded the street so severely that water reached knee height in the middle of the road, according to Lee Olsen, general manager at Waldo's Restaurant and Bar, who called it one of the worst floodings he has seen in 20 years.

The flooding has become a recurring problem tied to daily afternoon thunderstorms. Ocean Drive also flooded on Monday. Aubrey Moxley, who works at Allure Gallery across the street, said the entire street flooded in less than 30 minutes of rain this week. The flooding creates dangerous conditions for employees and threatens to cripple businesses by preventing customers from reaching the beach and shops along the strip.

The City of Vero Beach Public Works Department said pump stations and drainage infrastructure are working but are only designed to handle 1 inch of rainfall per hour. Recent storms exceeded that capacity, delivering 2 or more inches of rainfall in an hour. To fix the flooding, staff said the city would need to rebuild the road and make drainage improvements.

The city has no improvement project planned for Ocean Drive at this time. Olsen expressed concern about what a major storm could bring to ground-level businesses along the street and questioned where the city draws the line between cost and damage to local businesses.

hero.headline: Vero Beach utility bills to jump 47% by 2029 as city approves four-year rate increases
hero.body:
Vero Beach utility customers will face significant bill increases over the next four years after both the city's Utility Commission and City Council unanimously approved a comprehensive rate increase plan to fund major infrastructure improvements. The Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to increase water and sewer rates beginning on Oct. 1. A typical residential customer using 4,000 gallons per month currently pays $83.54 for combined water and sewer service. By 2029, that same bill will reach $122.45 monthly, an increase of nearly $39 per month, or 46.7% over current rates.

The rate increases stem from a $217 million capital improvement program planned through 2030. The centerpiece is a new Water Reclamation Facility currently under construction in Vero Beach. To finance the project, the city plans to issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027. The bonds are structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate, creating average annual debt service of approximately $8.66 million. An additional $42.3 million in grants will also support the project. The bond amount represents a significant jump from earlier projections. A 2022 rate study anticipated an $80 million bond issuance, but that figure has grown by $45 million due to cost escalation.

Water rates will increase 10% in fiscal year 2027, 7.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 5% in each of the following two years. Wastewater rates face steeper increases: 15% in both fiscal years 2027 and 2028, 10% in 2029, and 5% in 2030. Reclaimed water customers will see the largest percentage increases at 25% in both 2027 and 2028, followed by 5% annual increases. Beyond capital construction, the utility's operating expenses continue climbing at an average annual rate of 4.1%. Operating costs will grow from approximately $25.6 million in fiscal year 2026 to more than $32 million by 2030.

Currently, Vero Beach's combined bill of $83.54 falls below the regional average of $89.47 for similar usage. However, once the 2027 increases take effect, Vero Beach's $107.30 bill will exceed several neighboring utilities. Fort Pierce Utilities Authority currently charges $95.76 for the same 4,000-gallon usage level. Indian River County Sewer bills $67.70 for comparable service. The ordinance creates a new Wastewater Readiness-to-Serve Charge affecting property owners who receive city water service but use septic tanks while having public wastewater service available nearby. The charge starts at $40.85 monthly for typical residential customers as of Oct. 1, rising to $54.24 monthly by Oct. New rates take effect Oct. 1, with subsequent annual adjustments each Oct.

hero.headline: Colorado man indicted on attempted murder charges after Vero Beach shootout with deputies
hero.body:
A grand jury has indicted a Colorado man on charges of attempting to kill five deputy U.S. marshals during a shootout in Vero Beach. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida announced the indictment Thursday.

Thomas Earl Steffens, 72, was wanted on an arrest warrant in Colorado when he traveled by bus to Vero Beach. A U.S. Marshals fugitive task force tracked Steffens to Vero Beach on March 2. As law enforcement officers tried to arrest him at the intersection of 12th Street and Commerce Avenue, Steffens opened fire and struck one deputy in the chest and leg. Deputies returned fire, wounding Steffens before taking him into custody.

The task force involved three Indian River County deputies, one Martin County deputy and a deputy U.S. marshal. A witness said Steffens, who was wanted in Colorado on sexual assault and strangulation charges, fell out of his vehicle with blood on his face as deputies moved in to make the arrest.

Steffens faces five counts of attempted murder of a federal officer, one count of aggravated assault of a federal officer and one count of discharging a firearm during a crime of violence. If convicted, he faces up to life in prison.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police dispel active shooter rumor after SWAT operation on Southeast West Dunbrooke Circle
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department said Thursday it received no calls for service involving an active shooter after inaccurate social media posts claimed there was an active shooting near U.S. Highway 1. The activity residents saw was related to a search warrant executed by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office SWAT team at a home on Southeast West Dunbrooke Circle as part of an ongoing criminal investigation.

Some residents reported hearing gunshots, but law enforcement said the sounds were flash-bang devices used during the operation. The yelling heard in the area was officers giving commands to occupants leaving the home.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department gave no further details on the criminal investigation officers were responding to. The search warrant execution took place Thursday.

The false social media posts circulated throughout the day Thursday, prompting the police department to issue a public clarification about the SWAT operation.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce legal department loses three attorneys as city faces major development decisions
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce commissioners voted 3-2 to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while the city searches for a permanent replacement. The transition comes as the city faces several high-profile development issues expected to come before the City Commission.

hero.headline: Vero Beach utility bills to climb 47% by 2029 as city approves four-year rate increase
hero.body:
Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to increase water and sewer rates beginning Oct. 1, with bills rising nearly 47% over four years to fund a $217 million capital improvement program. A typical residential customer using 4,000 gallons per month currently pays $83.54 for combined water and sewer service. By 2029, that same bill will reach $122.45 monthly, an increase of nearly $39 per month.

The rate increases fund a new Water Reclamation Facility currently under construction in Vero Beach. The city plans to issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027, structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate, creating average annual debt service of approximately $8.66 million. An additional $42.3 million in grants will also support the project. The bond amount represents a significant jump from earlier projections, as a 2022 rate study anticipated an $80 million bond issuance.

Water rates will increase 10% in fiscal year 2027, 7.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 5% in each of the following two years. Wastewater rates face steeper increases of 15% in both fiscal years 2027 and 2028, 10% in 2029, and 5% in 2030. Reclaimed water customers will see the largest percentage increases at 25% in both 2027 and 2028, followed by 5% annual increases. Rate consultants at Raftelis identified additional operating costs of $3.07 million in fiscal year 2026 and $4.9 million in fiscal year 2029 compared to the prior 2022 rate study.

Currently, Vero Beach's combined bill of $83.54 falls below the regional average of $89.47 for similar usage, according to the Raftelis study. However, once the 2027 increases take effect, Vero Beach's $107.30 bill will exceed several neighboring utilities. Fort Pierce Utilities Authority currently charges $95.76 for the same 4,000-gallon usage level. Indian River County Sewer bills $67.70 for comparable service. The ordinance also creates a new Wastewater Readiness-to-Serve Charge affecting property owners who receive city water service but use septic tanks while having public wastewater service available nearby, starting at $40.85 monthly for typical residential customers as of Oct. 1.

cards.headline: Colorado man indicted on attempted murder charges after Vero Beach shootout with deputies
cards.teaser: A grand jury indicted a 72-year-old Colorado man on attempted murder charges after he allegedly opened fire on law enforcement officers attempting to arrest him in Vero Beach in March.
cards.body:
A grand jury indicted Thomas Earl Steffens, 72, on five counts of attempted murder of a federal officer, one count of aggravated assault of a federal officer and one count of discharging a firearm during a crime of violence. The indictment was announced Thursday by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida. Steffens was wanted on an arrest warrant in Colorado when he traveled by bus to Vero Beach.

Marshals fugitive task force tracked Steffens to Vero Beach on March 2. As law enforcement officers tried to arrest him at the intersection of 12th Street and Commerce Avenue, Steffens allegedly opened fire, striking one of the deputies in the chest and leg. Deputies returned fire, resulting in a shootout that left Steffens wounded. Three Indian River County deputies, one Martin County deputy and a deputy U.S. marshal were involved in the incident.

Steffens was wanted in Colorado on sexual assault and strangulation charges. If convicted, he faces up to life in prison.

cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department received no calls for service involving an active shooter Thursday despite an inaccurate social media post circulating that claimed there was an active shooting near U.S. 1. The activity residents may have seen was related to a search warrant executed by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office SWAT team at a home on Southeast West Dunbrooke Circle as part of an ongoing criminal investigation.

Some residents reported hearing gunshots, but law enforcement said the sounds were flash-bang devices used during the operation. The yelling heard in the area was officers giving commands to occupants leaving the home. The Port St. Lucie Police Department gave no further details on the criminal investigation officers were responding to.

cards.headline: National Weather Service explains tornado warning timing after Port St. Lucie EF0 strike
cards.teaser: The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds came in Sunday evening, but the tornado had already dissipated by that point.
cards.body:
The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds started to come in Sunday evening in Port St. Lucie, but at the point the warning was issued, the tornado had already dissipated. Because the tornado featured very shallow circulation, it was not picked up well by radar. Reports of the funnel cloud prompted the warning of the EF0 tornado that became a waterspout at one point.

Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said Sunday's event was unique because it was on the ground for 10 to 15 minutes, which is not something typically seen during summer months. The tornado was one of the typical summer afternoon thunderstorms that generated a brief and weak tornado with winds of 60 to 70 mph. Ulrich said the event is a good reminder that Mother Nature will always throw curveballs regardless of the time of year.

The National Weather Service is in charge of issuing tornado warnings and says once it is able to detect a tornado, it will always issue a tornado warning. The agency says to make sure you have multiple ways to receive these warnings to keep you and your loved ones safe.

hero.headline: Colorado man indicted on attempted murder charges after Vero Beach shootout with deputies
hero.body:
A grand jury has indicted a Colorado man accused of attempting to shoot and kill five deputy U.S. Marshals during a March 2 confrontation in Vero Beach. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida announced the indictment Thursday.

As law enforcement officers tried to arrest him at the intersection of 12th Street and Commerce Avenue, Steffens opened fire, striking one deputy in the chest and leg. Deputies returned fire, wounding Steffens before taking him into custody.

Three Indian River County deputies, one Martin County deputy and a deputy U.S. marshal were involved in the incident. A witness said Steffens, who was wanted in Colorado on sexual assault and strangulation charges, fell out of his vehicle with blood on his face as deputies moved in to make the arrest.

Steffens now faces five counts of attempted murder of a federal officer, one count of aggravated assault of a federal officer and one count of discharging a firearm during a crime of violence. If convicted, he faces up to life in prison.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce legal department shakeup raises questions on development decisions
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce faces uncertainty in its legal department as the city attorney's contract ends, the assistant city attorney resigns, and a temporary attorney prepares to leave, all while major development proposals loom.
cards.body:
A major transition inside Fort Pierce's legal department is raising questions about who will help guide the city through several high-profile development issues expected to come before the City Commission. The uncertainty follows the City Commission's decision not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract. At the same time, Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman has resigned, and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month, leaving the city searching for new legal leadership. This week, commissioners voted 3-2 to move forward with appointing Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while a search is conducted for a permanent replacement.

Commissioner Michael Broderick argues the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions. Broderick pointed specifically to future development proposals on South Hutchinson Island. Among the issues he expects to surface are potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. Broderick said removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island. Broderick voted against Wallace's appointment, saying the dual role of assistant city manager and charter officer creates conflicts. Wallace previously worked in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager.

Meanwhile, the commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Rene Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney. The agreement authorizes up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process. The search for a permanent city attorney is expected to continue over the coming months.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie High football player jailed on immigration detainer after school zone speeding stop
hero.body:
A Port St. Lucie High School football player has spent more than a week in the St. Lucie County Jail on an immigration detainer after a traffic stop for speeding through a school zone put him on federal immigration enforcement's radar. Emmanuel Nelson, 18, was stopped on Southeast Lennard Road near Southeast Grand Drive and Southeast Union Park Drive on the morning of August 19 after Deputy Daigneault clocked him driving 45 miles per hour in a 20-mile-per-hour school zone. Nelson was cited for unlawful speed in a school zone, a civil infraction that does not require a court appearance.

ICE arrested Nelson on August 22, three days after the traffic citation, during what the agency called an enforcement operation before transferring him to ICE custody. In a statement, an ICE spokesman described Nelson as an immigrant from Haiti living in the country illegally. ICE said Nelson entered the United States legally on January 16, 2016, but later violated the terms of his admission. He remains in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

On the football field, Nelson is a rising senior on the Port St. Lucie High School defense, according to comments head coach Everette Alford made in May. Nelson played in the August 14 Kickoff Classic against Fort Pierce Central High School, five days before he was cited and taken into custody.

ICE's statement also pointed to the agency's push for self deportation, telling immigrants in the country illegally that the government is offering money and a flight home through its CBP Home app, and warning of arrest and removal for those who do not take the offer. CBS12 plans to speak to Alford and Nelson's teammates.

cards.headline: Corgi found three streets away after Port St. Lucie tornado
cards.teaser: A six-year-old corgi went missing after an EF-0 tornado struck the Bay St. Lucie community in Port St. Lucie, forcing open the front door of her owner's home and causing damage throughout the house.
cards.body:
Luna, a six-year-old corgi, went missing after an EF-0 tornado struck the Bay St. Lucie community in Port St. Lucie and pushed open the front door of owner Molly Wing-Berman's home. The tornado made a big hole in the wall, took all the mail and items from surfaces, went out the back door, which was also locked, and put it in the pool, Berman said.

Berman had already gone to her laundry room for safety with her 2-year-old rescue dog, Enzo, as the tornado approached. Neighbors eventually found Luna three streets away.

Luna was shaking all over and has not really left Berman's side since. She has been sleeping very close to Berman. Luna now has a new nickname: Luna ToTo.

cards.body:
The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds started to come in Sunday evening in Port St. Lucie. At the point in which the warning was issued, the tornado had already dissipated. The tornado featured very shallow circulation and was not picked up well by radar. Reports of the funnel cloud are what prompted the warning of the EF-0 tornado that became a waterspout at a point.

Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said the event was unique because it was on the ground for a little bit. Ten to fifteen minutes is not something typically seen during the summer months, but it was one of the typical summer afternoon thunderstorms that generated a brief and weak tornado that had winds of 60 to 70 mph. Ulrich said it is a good reminder that Mother Nature will always throw curveballs regardless of the time of year.

hero.headline: Martin County deputies capture Fort Pierce man after hours-long swamp search following Palm City hit-and-run
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies captured a hit-and-run suspect Wednesday evening after searching for more than two hours through miles of swamp along the Martin County-St. Lucie County line. Deputies arrested 39-year-old Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce just before 6:15 p.m. Wednesday, pulling him from the murky swamp water in handcuffs. Both Daceus and the deputies who tracked him down were drenched from the water after the extended search.

The incident began with a hit-and-run crash in Palm City near Southwest Rivers End Way. Investigators say Daceus fled the scene and ran through the Windstone community before disappearing into a large swampy area near the county line. His disappearance sparked a large-scale search involving Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies, K-9 teams, aviation units, drone operators, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officers, and Port St. Lucie Police Department.

The search lasted more than two hours as helicopters circled overhead and officers established a perimeter around nearby neighborhoods. The significant law enforcement presence forced the closure of parts of Southwest Murphy Road and temporarily prevented some residents from returning home. The sheriff's office said the coordinated effort ultimately paid off, with technology playing a key role in locating Daceus.

Court records show Daceus previously had only a handful of traffic-related violations in Indian River County, including driving with a suspended license. Daceus was being booked into the Martin County Jail Wednesday evening. Investigators are continuing to review the case and determine what charges he will ultimately face.

cards.headline: Two men arrested in monthlong string of car burglaries across Martin County
cards.teaser: Martin County Sheriff's Office arrested two 19-year-old men on 36 charges each following a nearly monthlong investigation into car burglaries in multiple neighborhoods, including gated communities.
cards.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office arrested Stephen Ivan Morris and Shaun Alexander Bilbrey following a nearly monthlong investigation into a string of car burglaries across neighborhoods in Martin County. Both face 36 charges of grand theft, armed burglary, larceny and traveling to commit a burglary. Both were booked into the Martin County Jail on Tuesday.

The investigation into burglaries affecting multiple neighborhoods, including gated communities, began in early August. With assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office SWAT team and Criminal Investigations Division, Martin County detectives served warrants at the St. Lucie County homes of Morris, 19, and Bilbrey, 19. The two men allegedly committed 15 burglaries and stole at least 7 firearms. They also allegedly committed a burglary when they went into an open garage and stole a golf cart and drove it around the neighborhood to commit car burglaries.

The car burglaries happened in Hobe Sound, Palm City and two areas in Stuart, including the Stuart Yacht and Country Club. Sheriff John Budensiek says the two men may have committed other car burglaries that have not been reported yet because the victims are unaware their cars were burglarized. One firearm was stolen in Hobe Sound and then traded at a gas station for cash or some kind of transaction, and the sheriff's office does not know where that firearm is.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce appoints deputy city manager as interim city attorney amid legal department shakeup
hero.body:
Fort Pierce City Commission voted 3-2 this week to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while the city searches for a permanent replacement. The move follows the commission's decision not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract. Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman has resigned and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month.

Commissioner Michael Broderick voted against the appointment and raised concerns about the timing of the departures. Broderick said Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions in the coming months, particularly on South Hutchinson Island. He expects future proposals to include potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. Removing those restrictions could clear the way for taller development on the island.

Wallace previously worked in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager. Supporters said her legal background and familiarity with city operations provide continuity while the city loses much of its legal staff. Broderick argued the appointment creates a conflict. "So what the city commission did against my protests is they appointed the assistant city manager to now be a charter officer in the city of Fort Pierce," Broderick said. "In my opinion, that reeks of duplicity and multiple bosses you need to report to. I'm not sure how that is even possible to do."

The commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Rene Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney. The agreement authorizes up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process. City officials expect the interim appointment to return to the commission in the form of a formal contract and resolution. The search for a permanent city attorney is expected to continue over the coming months.

hero.headline: Vero Beach woman billed $922 for electricity after fire destroys home
hero.body:
A Vero Beach woman received a bill from Florida Power & Light for $922 in electricity charges more than a month after a fire destroyed her home and cut off her power. Debbie Drennan said the July 5 fire started in the early morning hours, destroying her home's carport and kitchen.

Drennan said she received the bill a month later that included charges for the time after the home had no service. She called FPL multiple times but could not get answers. The company even contacted her to say they were coming to disconnect her service for nonpayment.

After WPBF 25 News contacted FPL on Wednesday, the company reached out to Drennan. In an email, FPL apologized for the frustration and explained that the charge was due to an estimated bill because their system could not communicate with her meter. That meter was melted during the fire.

The company agreed to remove the $922 charge. Drennan said now that the issue with FPL has been resolved, she and her family can focus on repairing their home.
hero.article_text: More than a month after fire ripped through her Vero Beach home, Debbie Drennan said she received a bill from Florida Power Light charging her for electricity for weeks after her power had been cut off. The fire started in the early morning hours of July 5, destroying the home's carport and kitchen. “I’ve never been through anything like this. I mean, it was traumatic,” Drennan said. Drennan said the situation worsened a month later when she received a bill for power, including for the time after they had no service. And I’m like, 'What?' So, I looked at the dates, and it was after the fire. There was no electricity whatsoever,” she said. Drennan said she called FPL multiple times but could not get answers. She added that the company even contacted her to say they were coming to disconnect her service for nonpayment. Well, you just come on.' So, when he got here, I’m like, 'Sir, what are you disconnecting? Because there’s nothing to disconnect,'” Drennan said. After WPBF 25 News contacted FPL on Wednesday, the company said it could not discuss a customer’s account but later reached out to Drennan. In an email, FPL apologized for the frustration and explained that the charge was due to an "estimated bill" because their "system could not communicate" with her meter. That meter was melted during the fire. The company agreed to remove the charge. "At least the $922 is gone. Thanks to you guys.” Drennan said now that the issue with FPL has been resolved, she and her family can focus on repairing their home. cards.headline: National Weather Service explains tornado warning issued after Port St. Lucie tornado
cards.teaser: The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after an EF-0 tornado struck Port St. Lucie on Sunday evening, but the warning came after the tornado had already dissipated.
cards.body:
The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds started to come in Sunday evening in Port St. Lucie. At the point the warning was issued, the tornado had already dissipated. The tornado featured very shallow circulation and was not picked up well by radar, so reports of the funnel cloud prompted the warning of the EF-0 tornado that became a waterspout at a point.

Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said the tornado was on the ground for 10 to 15 minutes, which is not typical during the summer months. The tornado formed from a summer afternoon thunderstorm and had winds of 60 to 70 mph. "It was one of your typical summer afternoon thunderstorms that generated a brief and weak tornado that had winds of 60-70 mph, which is still pretty impactful to communities," Ulrich said. "And its a good reminder that Mother Nature will always throw us curveballs regardless of the time of year."

The National Weather Service is in charge of issuing tornado warnings. Once the National Weather Service is able to detect a tornado, it will always issue a tornado warning. The National Weather Service says residents should make sure they have multiple ways to receive warnings to keep themselves and their loved ones safe.

hero.headline: Martin County commissioners advance moratorium on data center development
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday to advance a discussion of a potential moratorium on data center development after residents voiced concerns about hyperscale facilities and their impact on the community. Commissioners voted 4-1 to place a discussion of a possible moratorium on data center development considerations on the agenda for their next meeting. If approved, the pause would give commissioners time to determine what rules and regulations they want to impose on data center projects.

Martin County resident Ann Vandersteel said she worries the nationwide surge in hyperscale data center development threatens the character of her community. She and other residents urged commissioners to act before projects move forward. Residents raised concerns about the impact data centers could have on air quality, noise pollution, water usage and electrical infrastructure.

Commissioner Edward Ciampi called for a moratorium during the meeting. He asked staff to bring forward an agenda item for a moratorium giving the commission the opportunity to have a year to bring forward experts and opinions. Commissioner Eileen Vargas noted the timeline could be flexible depending on how the review unfolds.

Vandersteel said during public comment that her biggest fear is that hyperscale data centers will disrupt and turn rural Martin County into a hyperscale data center campus. One resident said Martin County is not an industrial sacrifice zone. Another resident said residents should not have to discover the consequences after a project has been approved and built.

hero.headline: Palm City hit-and-run suspect pulled from swamp after hours-long manhunt
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office captured a hit-and-run suspect Wednesday evening after a more than two-hour search through miles of swamp along the Martin County-St. Lucie County line. Deputies pulled 39-year-old Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce from murky swamp water in handcuffs near the Windstone community off Southwest Rivers End Way in Palm City. Both Daceus and the deputies who tracked him down were drenched from the swamp water.

The manhunt began after Daceus fled the scene of a hit-and-run crash in the area of Southwest Rivers End Way. Investigators say he ran through the Windstone community before disappearing into a large swampy area near the county line. His flight sparked a large-scale search involving Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies, K-9 teams, aviation units, drone operators, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officers, and Port St. Lucie Police Department officers.

The search lasted more than two hours as helicopters circled overhead and officers established a perimeter around nearby neighborhoods. The significant law enforcement presence forced the closure of parts of Southwest Murphy Road and temporarily prevented some residents from returning home. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, who lives nearby, witnessed the operation. The sheriff's office said technology played a key role in locating Daceus.

Court records show Daceus previously had only a handful of traffic-related violations in Indian River County, including driving with a suspended license. He was being booked into the Martin County Jail Wednesday evening. Investigators are continuing to review the case and determine what charges he will ultimately face.

cards.headline: Two Port St. Lucie men arrested in Martin County burglary spree, 13 cases closed
cards.teaser: Martin County Sheriff's Office detectives arrested two 19-year-old Port St. Lucie men in connection with a string of burglaries that targeted gated communities and resulted in the theft of multiple firearms.
cards.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Detectives arrested Stephen Ivan Morris, 19, and Shaun Alexander Bilbrey, 19, both of St. Lucie County, on multiple charges after solving an ongoing burglary case involving the theft of multiple firearms from several neighborhoods, including gated communities. Detectives said the burglaries began in early August and as they worked to piece the cases together, they identified commonalities that ultimately led them to Morris and Bilbrey.

With assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office SWAT Team and the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Criminal Investigations Division, Martin County detectives served simultaneous search warrants early Wednesday morning at the homes of both men. The sheriff's office said multiple stolen firearms were recovered and they were able to close at least 13 cases.

hero.headline: Martin County commissioners set vote on data center moratorium after residents voice concerns
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted 4-1 Tuesday to place a discussion of a possible moratorium on data center development on the agenda for their next meeting, responding to residents who voiced concerns about hyperscale facilities and their impact on the community. If approved, the pause would give commissioners time to determine what rules and regulations they want to impose on data center projects.

Several residents showed up at the commission meeting to urge action before projects move forward. Martin County resident Ann Vandersteel said she worries the nationwide surge in hyperscale data center development threatens the character of her community. She said her biggest fear is that hyperscale facilities will turn rural Martin County into a data center campus. Other residents raised concerns about the impact data centers could have on air quality, noise pollution, water usage and electrical infrastructure.

Commissioner Edward Ciampi called for a moratorium during the meeting and asked staff to bring forward an agenda item giving the county a year to bring in experts and gather opinions. Commissioner Eileen Vargas noted the timeline could be flexible depending on how the review unfolds, saying the one-year timeframe is not hard and fast if the county needs to continue looking at more information.

Vandersteel said she left the meeting feeling cautiously optimistic about the commissioners' response. Residents told commissioners during public comment that Martin County is not an industrial sacrifice zone and that residents should not have to discover the consequences after a project has been approved and built. One resident told commissioners that a lot of people are worried and concerned and that it is imperative that commissioners do their homework.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce appoints interim city attorney as legal staff exits amid pending development decisions
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce commissioners voted 3-2 to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while the city searches for a permanent replacement following the departure of three attorneys.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce commissioners voted 3-2 this week to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while a search is conducted for a permanent replacement. The City Commission decided not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract, Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman has resigned, and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month.

Commissioner Michael Broderick voted against the appointment and said the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions. Broderick said there are several very volatile projects that are slated to come in front of the city commission in short order and the city has no independent legal representation to deal with that on behalf of the city commission. He pointed specifically to future development proposals on South Hutchinson Island, including potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density.

Supporters of the appointment said Wallace's experience in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager makes her well-positioned to step into the role and help keep city business moving. The commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Rene Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney, authorizing up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process.
cards.article_text: A major transition inside Fort Pierce's legal department is raising questions about who will help guide the city through several high-profile development issues expected to come before the City Commission. The uncertainty follows the City Commission's decision not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract. At the same time, Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman has resigned, and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month, leaving the city searching for new legal leadership. This week, commissioners voted 3-2 to move forward with appointing Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while a search is conducted for a permanent replacement. For Commissioner Michael Broderick, the concern isn't just staffing. He argues the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions. "There are several very volatile projects that are slated to come in front of the city commission in short order, and we really have no independent legal representation to be able to deal with that on behalf of the city commission, in my opinion," Broderick told CBS12 News. Broderick pointed specifically to future development proposals on South Hutchinson Island. Among the issues he expects to surface are potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. Broderick said removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island. The debate over development was one of several issues discussed as commissioners considered Wallace's appointment. See also: 2 arrested in string of car burglaries in Martin County Wallace previously worked in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager. Supporters said that experience makes her well-positioned to step into the role and help keep city business moving while a nationwide search for a permanent city attorney gets underway. Broderick voted against the appointment. "So what the city commission did against my protests is they appointed the assistant city manager to now be a charter officer in the city of Fort Pierce," Broderick said. "In my opinion, that reeks of duplicity and multiple bosses you need to report to. I'm not sure how that is even possible to do." Supporters of the move countered that Wallace's legal background and familiarity with city operations provide continuity at a time when the city is losing much of its legal staff. Meanwhile, the commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Renée Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney. The agreement authorizes up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process. City officials expect the interim appointment to return to the commission in the form of a formal contract and resolution. The search for a permanent city attorney is expected to continue over the coming months.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man charged with manslaughter after BB gun shooting
cards.teaser: A 36-year-old Fort Pierce man faces manslaughter charges after police say he fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun Saturday near an elementary school.
cards.body:
Jabari Cowart has been charged with manslaughter after Fort Pierce police say he fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday in the 2900 block of Avenue G. Police said a group of men in their 30s had been shooting a BB gun at trees when Cowart asked to use the weapon and later pointed it at one of the men before pulling the trigger. The victim fell to the ground and officers were called to the scene.

Ken Noble, marketing manager at The Tactical Store in Fort Pierce, said BB guns can be extremely dangerous. Noble explained that BB guns can cause serious injury or death because they fire metal projectiles at high speed. He said anything moving fast enough can penetrate skin and hit vital spots.

Cowart is being held at the St. Lucie County jail. Noble advised that people should not point any weapon at anyone and should follow safety procedures when handling firearms, including BB guns.

hero.headline: Martin County deputies capture Palm City hit-and-run suspect after hours-long swamp search
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies captured a hit-and-run suspect Wednesday evening after searching for more than two hours through miles of swamp along the Martin County-St. Lucie County line. The suspect fled a hit-and-run incident in the area of Southwest Rivers End Way in Palm City and was last seen running westbound into the Windstone Community.

The sheriff's office announced just before 6:15 p.m. Wednesday that the suspect was in law enforcement custody. The sheriff's office confirmed the suspect's identity as 39-year-old Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce. Deputies described him as a Black man wearing a black shirt with blue writing on the back and black pants.

Multiple K-9 units were deployed in the search along with air support to establish a large perimeter. The Martin County Sheriff's Office received assistance from its aviation, drone, and K-9 units, the Port St. Lucie Police Department and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officers.

The sheriff's office said the manhunt lasted more than two hours through the large swamp area spanning the county line. Deputies used multiple tracking methods to locate Daceus in the difficult terrain before taking him into custody Wednesday evening.

cards.headline: All 36 Border Collies from Palm City case surrendered to Humane Society, adoptions begin Sept. 1
cards.teaser: All 36 Border Collies removed from a Southwest Alligator Street home in Palm City earlier this month have been legally surrendered, clearing the way for adoptions beginning Sept. 1.
cards.body:
All 36 Border Collies removed from a Southwest Alligator Street home in Palm City on Aug. 10 have been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Investigators found the dogs living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste.

Shelter staff have removed the dogs' matted fur and cleaned away layers of dried feces as the animals recover. The dogs have received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasites. Two of the Border Collies are still struggling, are very withdrawn and don't make eye contact, while others are perking up and appear to be friendly.

Adoption applications for the Border Collies will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society's website and Facebook page. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. Paige ODonnell, 62, was arrested in the case and faces 72 charges including 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty. Her bond was set at $270,000.
cards.article_text: All 36 Border Collies removed from a Palm City home earlier this month have now been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast , clearing the way for medical evaluations and eventual adoptions. "They've come a very, very long way. I can't believe from when they've started to where they are now," said Sarah Fisher, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast Spokesperson. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from a home on Southwest Alligator Street, where investigators said they found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste. "You know, when they came in, they were very, very terrified. They were saturated in urine and feces," said Lori Tucker, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, Director of Operations. Since then, shelter staff have removed the dogs’ matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. They've received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasites. Tucker says two of the Border Collies are still struggling, are very withdrawn and don't make eye contact. Others are perking up already and appear to be super friendly. "I distinctly remember the second day that I came in and the first dog wagged its tail at me and for me, that was, I'll never forget that moment. I will never forget that moment. It was amazing," Tucker said as she fought back tears. Paige O’Donnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released. See also: Stuart shakeup, Mayor removed, city manager fired in dramatic end to commission meeting The Humane Society said it will complete medical testing and behavioral evaluations so potential adopters have clear information about each dog’s needs. The dogs will also be spayed or neutered, microchipped and vaccinated on a phased schedule. Some of the Border Collies will need additional veterinary care in the months ahead. "We've seen a lot of organ abnormalities and we think they're just like, defects from probably inbreeding. So we think that it's going to be a long road ahead of them," Fisher said. Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society’s website and Facebook page . The shelter said applicants will be carefully screened to find appropriate placements. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. The shelter is asking people not to call about the dogs so its phone lines remain available for urgent needs. While it does not need pet food or supplies at this time, it is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund to help cover veterinary care for the Border Collies and other shelter animals.

hero.headline: New Florida emergency chief inherits 41-day overdue accounting for disaster fund
hero.body:
Florida's new emergency management director Jared Perdue took control of an agency that failed to deliver a required financial report on the state's Emergency Preparedness and Response Fund, now 41 days past its legal deadline. A dozen Democratic lawmakers wrote to Perdue on Aug. 25 saying the Florida Division of Emergency Management never provided the quarterly accounting mandated under SB 7040, which required the first report by July 15. The report must detail the fund's projected year-end balance, cash-flow statements, federal reimbursements, an itemized list of purchased assets and unpaid invoices.

The fund has faced mounting scrutiny after more than $4.7 billion flowed through it since 2022, prompting lawmakers to debate tighter controls. Lawmakers say approximately $566 million was spent on immigration enforcement during the last fiscal year. An earlier FDEM annual report showed more than $573 million in immigration-related spending since 2023, including detention facilities, aircraft, vehicles and deployments of Florida personnel to Texas. FDEM told lawmakers it transmitted information on July 28, but the legislators said the materials consisted of five spreadsheets cataloging disaster spending and did not include the inventory, assets and pending invoices required under the new law.

Perdue, the longtime Florida Department of Transportation secretary, assumed the emergency management role after Kevin Guthrie resigned during hurricane season to join Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' unsuccessful campaign for governor. At his first press conference in the new role, Perdue promised both agencies would keep moving. Gov. Ron DeSantis said Wednesday that more than $100 million in federal immigration enforcement reimbursements has been repaid and that the overdue report is moving through the administration. DeSantis argued that Florida's multibillion-dollar reserves mean the state is not facing an immediate cash crunch.

The lawmakers' letter asks Perdue to provide the complete report by the end of August, explain the delay, account for outstanding contractor obligations and reconcile federal reimbursements that have been requested, approved, received, denied or remain pending. Rep. Anna Eskamani, D-Orlando, who organized the letter, said lawmakers remain hopeful Perdue will comply but indicated they are considering legal action. Florida has sought federal money to cover much of the immigration enforcement cost. Previous court filings raised questions about whether the state would receive the full $608 million reimbursement it expected and whether federal money could cover construction expenses.

cards.headline: Gov. DeSantis orders Florida flags to half-staff following Dolly Parton's death
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday ordered flags across Florida lowered to half-staff following the death of country music icon Dolly Parton.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday ordered flags across the state to be lowered to half-staff following the death of country music icon Dolly Parton. The governor's office said the order follows a directive from the president and applies to U.S. and Florida flags at all state and local government buildings, installations and grounds. The flags will remain at half-staff until sunset Sept. 1.

Parton died peacefully Tuesday in Nashville at age 80, according to her publicist. The Tennessee native became one of the most recognizable figures in country music during a career that spanned decades. She wrote hundreds of songs, including Jolene, Coat of Many Colors and I Will Always Love You, while also building a career in film, business and philanthropy. Parton was also known for founding the Imagination Library, which provides free books to children, and for opening Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce legal department shakeup leaves city without permanent attorney as development decisions loom
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce City Commission voted 3-2 this week to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while searching for a permanent replacement, following the departure of City Attorney Sara Hedges, whose contract was not renewed. Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman has resigned and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month, leaving the city without its legal leadership team.

Commissioner Michael Broderick raised concerns that the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions. He pointed specifically to future development proposals on South Hutchinson Island, including potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. Broderick said removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island.

Broderick voted against Wallace's appointment, arguing the dual role creates conflicts. He said appointing the assistant city manager to serve as a charter officer creates duplicity and multiple bosses to report to. Supporters of the move said Wallace's legal background and familiarity with city operations, including her previous work in the City Attorney's Office, provide continuity as the city loses much of its legal staff.

The commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Rene Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney, authorizing up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process. City officials expect the interim appointment to return to the commission in the form of a formal contract and resolution. The search for a permanent city attorney is expected to continue over the coming months.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie residents say tornado alerts came too late after EF-0 strikes neighborhood
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie residents are cleaning up after an EF-0 tornado touched down Sunday evening, and some say the weather alerts meant to warn them either arrived too late or never came at all. Aron Christiansen said his alert came in at 6:28 p.m., six minutes after the tornado had already passed his home. He said he was outside looking around when he got the alert. Neighbor Theresa Garone said she never received an alert, though her nephew's phone went off for a tornado.

The National Weather Service issued a tornado warning for portions of St. Lucie County after the initial tornado reports in Port St. Lucie. About 145,000 people were in the tornado warning area. The NWS said it had no known technical or dissemination issues with its systems related to this warning. The exact time an individual receives an alert can vary depending on the dissemination system, cellular provider, device settings, and local notification service.

Christiansen described the difference between preparing for a hurricane versus a tornado. He said hurricanes give days to prepare, but the tornado gave all of 10 seconds. One day after the storm, Christiansen was already working to clear the damage from his lanai.

The NWS said the tornado was a small, shallow circulation that was not well-sampled by radar. Because these circulations can be very small and short-lived, they can be difficult for radar to detect, particularly at greater distances from the radar site. Last year, an investigation uncovered flaws in Florida's tornado alert system, where thousands of people received alerts too late as a tornado struck Martin County in October 2024.

Was outside looking around and got the alert its like tornado warning, yeah, no kidding," Christiansen said.One day after the storm, Christiansen was already working to clear the damage."Made progress getting some of the lanai down," Christiansen said.He described the difference between preparing for a hurricane versus a tornado."Hurricanes — we get days to prepare, and tornado we had all of 10 seconds," Christiansen said.Neighbor Theresa Garone said she never received an alert."It's scary, it is, cause we don't get any warning for that," Garone said."My nephews phone went off for a tornado, but my phone never went off. so I don't know if it was like — I don't know what happened," Garone said.The NWS said about 145,000 people were in the Tornado Warning area, though the agency does not track how many individuals ultimately received alerts through the various dissemination systems.Once issued, the warning was distributed through multiple channels, including NOAA Weather Radio, the Emergency Alert System on television and radio, Wireless Emergency Alerts on compatible mobile devices, and local notification services such as ALERT St. The NWS said the exact time an individual receives an alert can vary depending on the dissemination system, cellular provider, device settings, and local notification service.The NWS said it had no known technical or dissemination issues with its systems related to this warning. cards.headline: Man charged with manslaughter after BB gun shooting in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: A 36-year-old man has been charged with manslaughter after Fort Pierce police say he fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday near an elementary school.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say Jabari Cowart, 36, fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday in the 2900 block of Avenue G, near an elementary school. Police said a group of men in their 30s had been shooting a BB gun at trees. Investigators believe Cowart asked to use the BB gun and later pointed it at one of the men before pulling the trigger. The victim fell to the ground, and officers were called to the scene.

Ken Noble, marketing manager at The Tactical Store in Fort Pierce, spoke about the dangers of BB guns. He said BB guns can be extremely dangerous because they shoot a piece of metal moving really fast. Noble explained that anything with a projectile can be a weapon, and anything moving fast enough can penetrate skin, hit vital spots, and can be very lethal. He said people should not point anything at anyone, and as long as safety procedures are followed, there should be nothing to worry about.

Cowart is being held at the St. Lucie County jail.

hero.headline: Two Port St. Lucie teens arrested in string of 15 burglaries and gun thefts across Martin County
hero.body:
Two 19-year-olds from Port St. Lucie were arrested after investigators connected them to 15 burglaries and a string of gun thefts across Martin County. The Martin County Sheriff's Office identified the suspects as Stephen Morris and Shaun Bilbrey. Investigators said the burglaries began on Aug. 1 in Hobe Sound, with the teens traveling by motorcycle and looking for unlocked vehicles across the county.

The thefts stretched from Hobe Sound, Palm City and Stuart, hitting a mix of gated and open communities. At the Stuart Yacht and Country Club, investigators said the teens went over a wall and stole a golf cart from a resident's garage. Surveillance video from the sheriff's office shows one of the suspects going through a car at the club. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said they used the golf cart to drive around the neighborhood and perpetrate their crimes.

When investigators searched the suspects' homes, they found seven stolen guns. Five were tied to the 15 burglaries. One gun was stolen from an unlocked car on Southeast Bahama Circle. Budensiek said they were simply pulling on door handles and grabbing what was easy to get.

Both Morris and Bilbrey are in the Martin County Jail with no bond. Each faces 36 charges, including armed robbery, larceny, and traveling to commit burglary. Neighbor Kevin Milliken, who has lived in the area for three years, said the arrest is changing his habits. His neighbor Carrie Boutwell said she will now be more mindful going forward.

cards.headline: Hit-and-run suspect captured after hours-long manhunt through swamp in Palm City
cards.teaser: A hit-and-run suspect is in custody after an exhaustive, hours-long manhunt through a large swamp along the Martin-St. Lucie County line.
cards.body:
A hit-and-run suspect is in custody after an exhaustive, hours-long manhunt through a large swamp along the Martin-St. Lucie County line, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The suspect fled from the scene of a hit-and-run crash in Palm City Wednesday and attempted to evade law enforcement by hiding in the swamp. The suspect was identified as Likenson Daceus, 39.

Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies and detectives, along with officers from Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and the Port St. Lucie Police Department, worked together for more than two hours to locate and apprehend the suspect. The search involved MCSO K-9s, aviation and drone units, as well as Port St. Lucie police's drone unit. Authorities said officers spent more than two hours navigating water and difficult terrain while the suspect continued trying to avoid capture.

cards.headline: All 36 Border Collies surrendered to Humane Society after Palm City rescue, adoptions open Sept. 1
cards.teaser: All 36 Border Collies removed from a Southwest Alligator Street home in Palm City earlier this month have been legally surrendered, clearing the way for adoptions.
cards.body:
All 36 Border Collies removed from a Palm City home earlier this month have now been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, clearing the way for medical evaluations and eventual adoptions. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from a home on Southwest Alligator Street, where investigators said they found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste.

Since then, shelter staff have removed the dogs' matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. They have received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasies. Lori Tucker, Director of Operations at the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said two of the Border Collies are still struggling, are very withdrawn and don't make eye contact. Others are perking up already and appear to be super friendly.

Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society's website and Facebook page. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. Paige ODonnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges, including 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000.

"They've come a very, very long way. I can't believe from when they've started to where they are now," said Sarah Fisher, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast Spokesperson. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from a home on Southwest Alligator Street, where investigators said they found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste. "You know, when they came in, they were very, very terrified. They were saturated in urine and feces," said Lori Tucker, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, Director of Operations. Since then, shelter staff have removed the dogs’ matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. They've received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasites. Tucker says two of the Border Collies are still struggling, are very withdrawn and don't make eye contact. Others are perking up already and appear to be super friendly. "I distinctly remember the second day that I came in and the first dog wagged its tail at me and for me, that was, I'll never forget that moment. I will never forget that moment. It was amazing," Tucker said as she fought back tears. Paige O’Donnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released. See also: Stuart shakeup, Mayor removed, city manager fired in dramatic end to commission meeting The Humane Society said it will complete medical testing and behavioral evaluations so potential adopters have clear information about each dog’s needs. The dogs will also be spayed or neutered, microchipped and vaccinated on a phased schedule. Some of the Border Collies will need additional veterinary care in the months ahead. "We've seen a lot of organ abnormalities and we think they're just like, defects from probably inbreeding. So we think that it's going to be a long road ahead of them," Fisher said. Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society’s website and Facebook page . The shelter said applicants will be carefully screened to find appropriate placements. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. The shelter is asking people not to call about the dogs so its phone lines remain available for urgent needs. While it does not need pet food or supplies at this time, it is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund to help cover veterinary care for the Border Collies and other shelter animals.
